artigo.texto: CATL Lays Out Solid-State Timetable as Australian Storage Launch and Hungary Court Win Broaden Its Base Published on 11/01/2026 at 18:40 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL has told investors it expects to turn out fully solid-state batteries in small production runs by 2027, a disclosure made on the interactive platform of the Shenzhen Stock Exchange on Tuesday. The company was careful to frame the target as small-series output rather than mass manufacturing, and stressed that it remains committed to research and development in the technology. The solid-state roadmap sits alongside an unusually busy stretch of partnership announcements. On 19 October, CATL agreed with Yinwang Intelligent Technologies and its battery-swapping subsidiary to build an intelligent system for exchanging electric-vehicle batteries. Three days later, on 22 October, it signed a deeper cooperation agreement with Beijing Automotive Group covering a swap system that, according to The Business Times, is designed to serve one million vehicles. BAIC will bring compatible models into CATL's Choco-Swap network, and its dealer network will help roll out the swapping stations. Heavy Trucks Get Their Own Platform Commercial vehicles are a separate front. CATL unveiled its Tianxing II battery platform for heavy trucks on 20 October; the company says its Qiji system can swap a truck battery in roughly five minutes. The build-out targets are ambitious: 900 heavy-truck swap stations in China by the end of 2026, 2,000 by 2027, and 10,000 over the longer term. A further agreement on 21 October with Shaanxi Transportation Holding Group covers swap infrastructure for heavy trucks as well as solar installations with storage and charging equipment along motorways, plus services spanning the battery life cycle and recycling. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? TENER+ Makes Its Debut in Australia Away from swapping, CATL introduced its TENER+ energy storage system, with 9 MWh of capacity, globally on Thursday at All Energy Australia. Media reports said the company also signed letters of intent at the show with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney to support large battery storage projects in Australia. In Hungary, a court on Friday dismissed a lawsuit brought by residents against the Debrecen battery plant, according to Reuters. The residents were no longer entitled to sue after the permitting documents were revised, and the court found no procedural irregularities in the approval process. The ruling removes a legal burden less than a month after trial production began. Revenue Outpaces Earnings The quarter's figures show top-line momentum running well ahead of the bottom line. Revenue for the third quarter of 2026 came in at RMB 165.22 billion, up 58.6% year on year. Net profit attributable to shareholders reached RMB 21.25 billion, a gain of 14.5% — leaving profit growth trailing revenue growth by a wide margin. artigo.texto: Parceiro institucional: (Envato/Envato) Colunista Publicado em 30 de outubro de 2026 às 11h00. Última atualização em 30 de outubro de 2026 às 12h01. Data centers podem adicionar centenas de megawatts de demanda em prazos muito menores do que os necessários para construir linhas, subestações ou novas usinas. Com a expansão da inteligência artificial, esse descompasso começa a mudar a forma de planejar grandes conexões ao sistema elétrico. A pergunta deixa de ser apenas quanto de infraestrutura será necessário construir e passa a importar também quanto da nova carga pode ser flexibilizada justamente nos períodos em que a rede enfrenta restrições. Um estudo da PSR para a região de Barueri, em São Paulo, ajuda a dimensionar esse efeito. Considerando o sistema em 2029, com 200 cenários de operação, a região comportaria cerca de 400 MW adicionais de carga no pior caso sem redução de consumo. Com flexibilidade equivalente a 1% da energia anual, essa capacidade sobe para aproximadamente 650 MW. Isso não significa que os 250 MW de flexibilidade substituam automaticamente a mesma quantidade de geração ou transmissão: o que isso mostra é que reduções de consumo concentradas nas horas críticas podem permitir melhor aproveitamento da infraestrutura existente e postergar ou evitar determinados reforços. Logo, os data centers são particularmente interessantes nesse debate. Além de baterias e sistemas próprios de backup, parte da carga computacional pode, em determinadas condições, ser deslocada ou modulada. Há ainda alternativas de resposta da demanda e agregação de recursos externos. Mas o valor da flexibilidade depende também da duração, frequência, velocidade de resposta e localização. Uma restrição na rede ocorre em determinado ponto e momento, e o recurso flexível precisa estar disponível justamente quando e onde produz benefício para o sistema, o que muda a economia da conexão. Dois consumidores com a mesma demanda máxima podem gerar impactos distintos sobre a rede se um deles puder reduzir consumo em situações críticas. Para o Brasil, isso abre espaço para analisar conjuntamente prazo de conexão, investimentos em rede e compromissos de flexibilidade. Também permite comparar economicamente essa alternativa com reforços de transmissão e distribuição, armazenamento ou outras soluções de expansão. O avanço dessa lógica depende, porém, de regras capazes de transformar flexibilidade técnica em recurso efetivamente utilizável pelo sistema. Isso exige medição verificável, remuneração compatível com a obrigação assumida, definição clara das condições de acionamento e coordenação entre planejamento, operação, transmissão, distribuição e mercado. Também será necessário reconhecer que a flexibilidade tem valor locacional. Um recurso disponível longe do ponto de restrição pode ter pouco efeito sobre o problema que limita uma nova conexão. Por isso, a análise econômica precisa estar associada à configuração real da rede e às horas em que o sistema enfrenta maior estresse. A questão para os próximos data centers, portanto, não será apenas quanta energia irão consumir. Será também quanto vale para o sistema a capacidade de consumir menos nas poucas horas em que a rede mais precisa disso.

artigo.texto: PJM approves two ENGIE battery storage projects totaling 1,660 MW under new expedited interconnection process PJM Interconnection has approved two large battery storage projects from ENGIE IR Holdings LLC as among the first accepted under its new Expedited Interconnection Track. The facilities — an 860-megawatt project in Crawford, Pennsylvania, and an 800-megawatt project in Morrow, Ohio — represent a combined 1,660 megawatts of storage capacity, with both slated to come online in mid-2029. PJM accepts ENGIE storage projects under expedited track The two ENGIE facilities are among the first three projects ever accepted under PJM’s Expedited Interconnection Track — a notable milestone for a process that didn’t exist until recently. These approvals mark its earliest real-world test. ENGIE IR Holdings LLC is the entity behind both projects. The Crawford, Pennsylvania facility comes in at 860 MW, while the Morrow, Ohio project adds another 800 MW. Together, they account for the vast majority of capacity approved under the new track so far. That two of the first three expedited approvals are storage projects — rather than traditional generation — says something about where the industry is heading. Both projects are scheduled to begin operations in mid-2029. That timeline is central to the whole point of the expedited process: getting large resources connected faster than the standard queue typically allows. Why PJM created the expedited interconnection process Electricity demand across the PJM region has been climbing steadily, and the pressure isn’t letting up. Data centers are a major driver, along with other large commercial and industrial facilities requiring significant, reliable power. PJM’s standard interconnection queue has struggled to keep pace. Backlogs have built up over the years, leaving developers waiting long stretches before their projects can connect to the grid — a real problem when demand is rising and new capacity is needed sooner rather than later. The Expedited Interconnection Track was designed specifically to cut through that bottleneck. It targets large generation and storage resources that can move quickly: projects already backed by a primary siting authority and capable of beginning operations within three years of approval. If a project is well-positioned and ready to move, there’s little reason to hold it in a slow-moving queue alongside projects at much earlier stages of development. What the approvals mean for grid capacity and storage development Adding 1,660 MW of battery storage to the PJM grid by mid-2029 is a meaningful contribution. PJM covers territory across 13 states and the District of Columbia, making it one of the largest electricity markets in the world — so the scale of these projects fits the region’s scope. Battery storage has been growing as a tool for grid operators. Approvals like these suggest that large-scale storage is becoming a more central part of how regions like PJM plan to meet rising demand. Storage can absorb excess generation and discharge it when demand peaks, a capability that gets more valuable as the grid evolves. That two of the first three expedited approvals are storage projects — rather than traditional generation — says something about where the industry is heading. Developers are clearly positioning battery storage as a fast-deployable, grid-ready resource. For ENGIE, getting two projects through early under this process puts the company in a strong position ahead of what could be a competitive window, since the track allows only up to 10 approvals per year. Scope and timeline of the Expedited Interconnection Track The Expedited Interconnection Track is explicitly temporary, designed as a short-term measure scheduled to end after 2027. That gives developers roughly two years to pursue approvals under this faster pathway before it closes. During 2026 and 2027, PJM can approve a maximum of 10 interconnection requests per year through this track. It’s a tight cap. With three projects already accepted — the two ENGIE facilities and one other — the available slots are already starting to fill. The track represents a meaningful, if limited, departure from PJM’s standard process, which has faced well-documented backlogs, with projects sometimes waiting years for studies and approvals. The expedited track doesn’t replace that system. It runs alongside it, offering a faster lane for projects that meet strict qualifying criteria: backing from a primary siting authority and the ability to come online within three years. That filters out early-stage or speculative projects, keeping the track focused on resources genuinely close to ready. What this means going forward To sum it up: PJM has approved two ENGIE battery storage projects — 860 MW in Crawford, Pennsylvania, and 800 MW in Morrow, Ohio — as part of the first wave of acceptances under its new Expedited Interconnection Track. Combined, they represent 1,660 MW of storage capacity expected online by mid-2029. The expedited process was created in response to growing electricity demand, particularly from data centers, and the chronic backlogs that have slowed PJM Inside Lines‘ standard interconnection queue. Capped at 10 approvals per year in 2026 and 2027, it ends after 2027. Three projects are approved, the window is still open, and the remaining capacity is finite. Developers with qualifying projects will be watching closely as the remaining slots come into play over the next two years. artigo.texto: LG CNS, a South Korean digital transformation and information technology services company, has completed construction of a 30 MW AI data center in Jakarta, Indonesia. The project was commissioned by Kuningan Mas Gemilang (KMG), a joint venture between Indonesia’s Cinarmas Group and South Korea’s Tuzarial Asset Management. According to an LG CNS press release, the facility is designed to support high performance computing (HPC) using next generation graphics processing units (GPUs) and marks the first time a South Korean company has directly built an AI data center overseas for a local customer. Hyun Shin-kyun, CEO, LG CNS, said, “Completion of the construction of the Indonesian AI data center will provide LG CNS’s domestically accumulated data center capabilities to overseas customers. It is a meaningful achievement that has proven business competitiveness in the global market. We will use this as a bridgehead to expand our AI data center and AI factory business in global markets, including the Asia-Pacific region, where demand for AI computing is rapidly increasing.” The data center’s power infrastructure can support loads exceeding 300 KW per rack, allowing it to accommodate multiple GPUs within a single rack. Redundant power systems, including backup supplies, are designed to maintain operations around the clock in the event of a disruption to the main electricity supply. Its cooling infrastructure combines air cooling with provisions for liquid cooling, which will be introduced in a subsequent construction phase to manage the heat generated by high density AI servers. Once completed, the data center’s total capacity is expected to reach 400 MW, positioning it among Indonesia’s largest AI data center facilities. The project also brought together capabilities from across the LG Group, including LG Electronics’ air conditioning systems and LG Energy Solution’s batteries, alongside LG CNS’ data center design, construction and operation expertise. LG CNS is also pursuing AI data center projects in other Asia-Pacific markets, including Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Japan, using its Indonesian project as a reference for overseas expansion. Beyond data center construction and operation, LG CNS has been expanding into modular data centers, GPU-as-a-Service (GPUaaS) and liquid cooling infrastructure. The company also plans to develop AI factory services that integrate AI platforms and infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Data centers viram pauta eleitoral nos EUA em 2026 Quase US$ 200 bilhões em projetos de data centers foram bloqueados ou atrasados nos EUA no primeiro semestre de 2026. O tema agora influencia disputas eleitorais. A expansão de data centers nos Estados Unidos deixou de ser um assunto restrito a engenheiros de infraestrutura e executivos de big techs. Em 2026, o tema se tornou uma questão eleitoral capaz de influenciar disputas legislativas nas eleições de meio de mandato, marcadas para 3 de novembro. Um relatório do Data Center Watch revelou que quase US$ 200 bilhões em projetos de data centers foram atrasados, paralisados ou bloqueados no primeiro semestre de 2026 por conta de oposição política e comunitária. O número é expressivo e sinaliza uma mudança na dinâmica entre o setor de tecnologia e a sociedade americana. Estados como Pensilvânia, Geórgia, Texas, Nova York e Virgínia já discutem novas regras de transparência e limitações para a construção acelerada dessas estruturas. Só na Virgínia, apelidada de “capital mundial dos data centers”, centenas de novos projetos estão planejados. Por que comunidades estão se opondo aos data centers A resistência não é apenas ambiental, embora preocupações com consumo de energia e recursos hídricos sejam centrais. O que move a oposição é uma sensação mais ampla de perda de controle. Moradores de diversas regiões relatam que grandes empresas de tecnologia fecham acordos com autoridades locais sem consulta pública, construindo instalações bilionárias antes que a comunidade consiga sequer protestar. Em alguns casos, regras de zoneamento tornam difícil identificar o que está sendo construído até que seja tarde demais. Pesquisadores e advogados de direitos humanos apontam que os data centers se tornaram a materialização física do medo e da raiva que parte da população sente em relação à classe tecnológica e ao ritmo acelerado da transformação digital. Como analisamos em nossa cobertura de tecnologia, a tensão entre inovação e impacto social é um tema recorrente, mas raramente atinge o nível de mobilização eleitoral que se observa agora nos EUA. Empregos temporários e promessas questionadas Um dos principais argumentos a favor dos data centers é a geração de empregos. Alguns sindicatos trabalhistas apoiam os projetos por conta das vagas prometidas durante a construção. Dados disponíveis, no entanto, mostram que esses empregos são majoritariamente temporários. Uma vez concluída a obra, a operação de um data center exige uma equipe muito menor. A comparação com o passado industrial americano é inevitável. Comunidades do chamado Cinturão da Ferrugem tinham orgulho de fábricas enormes e esteticamente questionáveis porque elas representavam emprego estável, prosperidade e futuro para as famílias. Data centers, por outro lado, oferecem uma promessa diferente: infraestrutura de ponta que beneficia empresas globais, mas que nem sempre traduz riqueza para a comunidade ao redor. Até figuras políticas alinhadas ao setor de tecnologia enfrentam resistência. Vivek Ramaswamy, por exemplo, foi vaiado ao defender data centers em Ohio, um estado tradicionalmente industrial. A rejeição atravessa linhas partidárias, como destacou a cobertura de analistas políticos americanos. Tanto eleitores republicanos quanto democratas demonstram desconforto com a falta de consentimento no processo. A desconexão entre o Vale do Silício e o restante do país A expansão dos data centers expõe uma fratura cultural que vai além de infraestrutura. Para quem trabalha com tecnologia, a inteligência artificial representa progresso, eficiência e oportunidade. Para uma parcela significativa da população americana, IA e data centers simbolizam ameaças: perda de empregos, concentração de riqueza e degradação ambiental. Essa desconexão não é nova, mas ganhou contornos mais agudos. Enquanto líderes de big techs discutem abertamente a possibilidade de a IA substituir trabalhadores ou até segmentos inteiros da força humana, famílias americanas enfrentam custo de vida crescente e insegurança econômica. Como abordamos em análises anteriores sobre IA e mercado de trabalho, o descompasso entre narrativa corporativa e realidade social tende a gerar reações políticas. Políticos locais já perceberam a oportunidade. Em Nova York, vereadores têm pressionado por maior responsabilização de executivos de tecnologia. A demanda por transparência e tributação mais pesada sobre grandes fortunas do setor tech ganhou tração, especialmente entre políticos que se identificam com pautas progressistas. O que isso significa para o setor de tecnologia O cenário coloca as big techs diante de um dilema operacional concreto. Com quase US$ 200 bilhões em projetos travados, a capacidade de expandir infraestrutura de IA nos EUA está comprometida no curto prazo. Isso pode acelerar a busca por locais alternativos, inclusive fora do país, e pressionar por modelos de negociação mais transparentes com comunidades locais. Para investidores e empresas que dependem dessa infraestrutura, o risco regulatório deixou de ser hipotético. Estados já trabalham em legislações específicas, e o tema promete ganhar ainda mais destaque conforme as eleições de novembro se aproximam. Como discutimos em nossa análise sobre regulação de tecnologia nos EUA, o ambiente político americano está se tornando menos permissivo para expansões sem consulta pública. A questão central não é se os data centers serão construídos, mas em que termos. A era da expansão silenciosa parece estar chegando ao fim. E o mercado de tecnologia precisará aprender a negociar com comunidades que, cada vez mais, exigem assento à mesa. artigo.texto: Gerdau e o boom de data centers: por que o aço surfou a onda da IA Expansão de data centers de IA nos EUA eleva demanda por aço longo e coloca a Gerdau em posição privilegiada. Analistas revisam projeções para cima. Quando se fala em inteligência artificial, o primeiro reflexo do mercado é pensar em chips, servidores e ações de tecnologia. Poucos investidores param para considerar o que sustenta fisicamente essa revolução: estruturas de aço, concreto e cabos que formam os data centers onde a IA de fato opera. É nesse elo menos óbvio da cadeia que a Gerdau aparece como uma das grandes beneficiárias. Analistas de um grande banco elevaram o preço-alvo das ações da siderúrgica de R$ 31 para R$ 35, reiterando recomendação de compra. O papel é apontado como a principal escolha no setor siderúrgico brasileiro. A tese se apoia em um argumento simples, mas poderoso: o mercado pode estar subestimando a capacidade de geração de caixa da Gerdau nos Estados Unidos. Data centers de IA impulsionam demanda por aço longo nos EUA O segmento de vigas e barras comerciais da Gerdau na América do Norte vive um momento atípico. O consumo aparente desses dois produtos cresceu cerca de 6,5% no acumulado do ano, mesmo com uma queda de aproximadamente 1% nos gastos totais com construção não residencial nos Estados Unidos. Essa divergência tem nome: data centers. Os gastos com construção desse tipo de instalação nos EUA avançaram 75% na comparação anual, segundo dados recentes. Embora representem apenas cerca de 5% do total gasto com construção não residencial, os data centers são intensivos em aço longo, exatamente o tipo de produto que a Gerdau fabrica e vende no mercado americano. Para quem acompanha o mercado financeiro, o dado relevante é a exposição desproporcional: os produtos da companhia têm maior penetração justamente nos segmentos de construção pesada que mais crescem. Hyperscalers devem acelerar investimentos até 2027 O ciclo de investimentos dos grandes provedores de serviços em nuvem, os chamados hyperscalers, está longe de desacelerar. As projeções apontam que o início de novas construções de data centers deve avançar cerca de 200% até 2027. Para a Gerdau, isso se traduz em demanda sustentada por anos. O ponto que o mercado parece ignorar, segundo os analistas, é que o crescimento da demanda deve superar qualquer pressão pelo lado da oferta. Existe, sim, preocupação com aumento de capacidade instalada e importações de aço nos EUA. Mas a aceleração do consumo, puxada pela construção de infraestrutura de IA, tende a absorver essa nova oferta sem comprimir margens. Essa dinâmica lembra, em escala diferente, o que aconteceu com o setor de infraestrutura tecnológica nos últimos anos, quando a corrida pela digitalização criou gargalos inesperados em setores tradicionais da economia real. Projeções financeiras revisadas para cima As novas estimativas são significativas. O EBITDA projetado para este ano foi elevado para R$ 13,9 bilhões, alta de 3% em relação à projeção anterior. Para 2027, a expectativa subiu 8%, chegando a R$ 15,2 bilhões. A margem EBITDA esperada para a operação na América do Norte em 2027 passou de 24% para 26,4%. É uma revisão relevante que reflete diretamente a leitura mais otimista sobre a demanda estrutural por aço longo no mercado americano. Outro fator que contribui para a revisão é o câmbio. Após a reeleição de Lula, a premissa cambial foi ajustada para um dólar a R$ 5,40, o que beneficia os resultados consolidados da Gerdau, já que boa parte da receita vem de operações dolarizadas. Nos múltiplos atuais, a Gerdau negocia a 3,5 vezes o EBITDA estimado para 2027, com um free cash flow yield de 14%. Para efeito de comparação, siderúrgicas globais costumam negociar a múltiplos entre 4 e 6 vezes, o que sugere espaço para reavaliação. O que os números recentes mostram na B3 A companhia vale R$ 47,8 bilhões na B3. Nos últimos doze meses, a ação acumula alta de 33%, um desempenho expressivo para um papel do setor de commodities em um ambiente de Ibovespa sob pressão. Em um dia recente de queda do índice, o papel chegou a subir 6,5%, sinalizando que o mercado começa a precificar a tese de demanda estrutural. Para o investidor que analisa ações na bolsa brasileira, o caso da Gerdau ilustra um padrão importante: grandes tendências tecnológicas criam oportunidades em setores que parecem distantes do epicentro da inovação. A revolução da IA não beneficia apenas quem fabrica chips. Beneficia quem fornece a estrutura física para que essa tecnologia exista. O elo esquecido entre IA e economia real A narrativa de investimento em inteligência artificial concentrou, nos últimos anos, a atenção do mercado em empresas de semicondutores, software e computação em nuvem. Mas toda infraestrutura digital precisa de infraestrutura física. Cada novo data center demanda milhares de toneladas de aço estrutural, e a escala dos projetos dos hyperscalers é sem precedentes. A Gerdau, com operações consolidadas nos EUA e foco em aço longo para construção pesada, está posicionada de forma quase acidental nesse cruzamento entre velha economia e nova tecnologia. Não foi uma aposta deliberada da gestão em IA. Foi a combinação certa de produto, geografia e timing de mercado. O risco, como sempre, existe. Uma desaceleração nos planos de investimento dos hyperscalers, mudanças na política comercial americana ou uma recessão nos EUA poderiam comprometer a tese. Mas, por enquanto, os dados apontam na direção oposta: a demanda cresce mais rápido do que a oferta consegue acompanhar. Para quem busca exposição à tese de IA fora das big techs, o aço pode ser a aposta mais contraintuitiva e, ao mesmo tempo, mais fundamentada do mercado. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentabilidade passada não é garantia de resultados futuros.

artigo.texto: Gerdau e o boom dos data centers: por que o aço surfou a onda da IA A expansão de data centers de IA nos EUA impulsiona a demanda por aço longo e coloca a Gerdau como uma das principais beneficiadas do ciclo de investimentos em infraestrutura. Quando o mercado fala em inteligência artificial, o reflexo imediato é pensar em chips, servidores e big techs. Mas existe uma camada física, feita de concreto e aço, que sustenta toda essa revolução. E é exatamente aí que a Gerdau aparece como uma das teses mais interessantes do momento na bolsa brasileira. Analistas do UBS BB acabam de elevar o preço-alvo das ações da siderúrgica de R$ 31 para R$ 35, ampliando também as projeções de resultado. A lógica por trás da revisão é direta: a explosão na construção de data centers nos Estados Unidos está criando uma demanda estrutural por aço longo que o mercado ainda não precificou adequadamente. Data centers de IA consomem aço em escala industrial Os gastos com construção de data centers nos Estados Unidos cresceram 75% na comparação anual, segundo dados compilados pelo UBS BB. Embora o segmento represente cerca de 5% do total de gastos com construção não residencial no país, sua intensidade no uso de aço longo é desproporcional. Os números reforçam essa tese. O consumo aparente de vigas e barras comerciais nos EUA avançou 6,5% no acumulado do ano, mesmo com uma queda de aproximadamente 1% nos gastos totais com construção não residencial. Essa divergência não é acidental. Ela reflete a força dos segmentos de construção pesada, justamente onde a Gerdau tem maior exposição. Como temos acompanhado na cobertura de tecnologia, os grandes provedores de nuvem, conhecidos como hyperscalers, estão acelerando investimentos em infraestrutura. A expectativa é que o início de novas construções avance cerca de 200% até 2027, criando um ciclo de demanda que pode durar vários anos. O mercado olha para o risco errado A narrativa dominante sobre siderurgia nos EUA gira em torno de riscos de oferta. Há preocupação com aumento de capacidade instalada e crescimento das importações. Esses são riscos reais, mas a análise do UBS BB sugere que o foco excessivo neles pode estar distorcendo a leitura sobre a Gerdau. A tese central é que o crescimento da demanda tende a superar qualquer pressão do lado da oferta. Os investimentos em data centers de IA não são um fenômeno cíclico passageiro. Empresas como Microsoft, Google e Amazon já sinalizaram planos de capex na casa das centenas de bilhões de dólares para os próximos anos, como detalhamos na editoria de finanças. Para os analistas, essa aceleração do consumo deve ser suficiente para absorver a nova capacidade e o aumento de importações, mantendo as margens da Gerdau em patamares elevados. A margem EBITDA esperada para a operação na América do Norte em 2027 foi revisada de 24% para 26,4%. Revisão de números e câmbio favorável O UBS BB agora projeta um EBITDA de R$ 13,9 bilhões para a Gerdau neste ano, 3% acima da estimativa anterior. Para 2027, a projeção subiu 8%, chegando a R$ 15,2 bilhões. A revisão reflete principalmente a perspectiva mais otimista para a operação norte-americana. Há também um componente cambial relevante. A nova premissa de câmbio adotada pelo banco é de R$ 5,40 por dólar, o que naturalmente beneficia os resultados consolidados da Gerdau, já que uma parcela significativa da receita é gerada em moeda americana. Nos múltiplos atuais, a companhia negocia a 3,5 vezes o EBITDA estimado para 2027, com um retorno de fluxo de caixa livre (free cash flow yield) de 14%. São números que chamam atenção mesmo em um ambiente de juros elevados no Brasil. A empresa vale R$ 47,8 bilhões na B3, com valorização de 33% nos últimos doze meses. A conexão entre aço e inteligência artificial O caso da Gerdau ilustra uma dinâmica que investidores mais atentos já começaram a mapear: os efeitos de segunda e terceira ordem da revolução da IA. Os beneficiários óbvios são fabricantes de chips e provedores de nuvem. Mas a cadeia de valor é muito mais extensa. Data centers precisam de estruturas físicas massivas. São galpões de centenas de milhares de metros quadrados, com fundações robustas, sistemas de refrigeração e infraestrutura elétrica de grande porte. Tudo isso demanda aço, e especificamente o tipo de aço longo que a Gerdau produz em suas operações nos Estados Unidos. Essa é uma leitura que tem ganhado tração entre analistas de infraestrutura. A ideia de que a corrida pela IA vai beneficiar setores tradicionais da economia real não é nova, mas os dados de construção nos EUA começam a confirmar a tese com números concretos. O que isso significa para o investidor A Gerdau se posiciona como uma espécie de pá e picareta da corrida do ouro da inteligência artificial. Enquanto o debate sobre valuations de empresas de tecnologia se acirra, a siderúrgica oferece exposição ao tema com múltiplos comprimidos e geração de caixa robusta. O risco, naturalmente, existe. Uma desaceleração nos planos de capex dos hyperscalers, mudanças na política comercial americana ou uma recessão nos EUA poderiam comprometer a tese. Mas o cenário base, ao menos por enquanto, favorece empresas que fornecem a infraestrutura física para a expansão digital. A ação subiu 6,5% em um dia de queda do Ibovespa, sinalizando que o mercado começa a prestar atenção nessa história. A pergunta agora é se o potencial de geração de caixa da operação americana já está nos preços ou se ainda há espaço para reavaliação. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentabilidade passada não é garantia de resultados futuros.

artigo.texto: Emerald to Develop 60 kWh Sodium-Ion Battery for Pickering Barn Microgrid Emerald Battery Labs will develop a 60 kWh sodium-ion battery for Issaquah’s Pickering Barn solar microgrid, although certification and procurement remain ahead. Published · 4 min read Emerald Battery Labs announced October 29 that it will develop a 60 kWh sodium-ion battery system for the Pickering Barn microgrid in Issaquah, Washington, pairing storage with an existing municipal solar array so the historic community facility can ultimately support critical loads during grid outages. The announcement advances the battery design and vendor stage, but the system is not yet certified, permitted, procured or operating. The project is supported in part by a $671,000 TransAlta Centralia Generation grant. Pickering Barn already has a 64.9 kW-DC solar array, while the proposed battery must still complete design work and obtain UL 9540, UL 9540A and UL 1973 certifications before deployment. Pickering Barn microgrid adds a sodium-ion design In its October 29 project announcement, Emerald said the grant will support development and deployment of a 60 kWh sodium-ion battery energy storage system integrated with the city’s existing solar and electrical hardware. The company’s work will cover sodium-ion integration, energy-management and battery-management communications, and system-level safety validation. Emerald also said it will support the City of Issaquah through permitting and procurement after finalizing the design and completing the required certifications. That sequence is significant. A selected chemistry and design partner do not make the battery operational. Certification, municipal procurement, permitting, installation, controls integration and commissioning remain ahead before the project can demonstrate islanded service. The city’s October council calendar separately identifies Agenda Bill 9256 for the TransAlta grant and Pickering Barn battery storage. The official record corroborates the municipal project and grant action, while the Emerald release supplies the new vendor, chemistry and 60 kWh design details. The battery would complete an islandable solar-plus-storage system Issaquah installed the first major energy component earlier in 2026. The city says its 65 kW Pickering Barn solar project is expected to generate 53.74 MWh annually and reduce municipal electricity costs by more than $6,000 per year. Solar generation alone does not establish outage operation. For the facility to separate from the utility grid, the final design will need an islanding strategy, appropriately configured inverters and controls, protection, switching and a defined set of critical loads. The 60 kWh energy rating also does not reveal how long the barn can operate during an outage. Duration depends on the battery’s usable capacity, inverter power rating, state-of-charge reserve, solar production, conversion losses and the size and priority of the loads that remain energized. Microgrid Media’s guide to microgrid battery sizing explains why kWh determines stored energy while kW determines how much instantaneous load the system can carry. Emerald and the city have not disclosed the proposed battery power rating or a verified outage-duration target. Sodium-ion changes the project’s technology risk Sodium-ion batteries replace lithium with more abundant sodium-based materials and are being developed for applications where cost, supply-chain diversity and thermal behavior may be more important than maximizing energy density. Emerald says its chemistry offers improved thermal stability, long cycle life and freedom from lithium and cobalt dependency. Those are manufacturer claims for the proposed product, not measured operating results from Pickering Barn. The certification plan is therefore central to the story. UL Solutions’ energy-storage certification guidance explains that UL 1973 addresses batteries for stationary and other applications, while UL 9540 covers complete energy-storage systems. UL 9540A is the test method used to evaluate thermal-runaway fire propagation. Completing those processes would not by itself prove long-term field performance, but it is an important prerequisite for safety review and deployment. The proposed system is much smaller than utility-scale battery projects, yet its public-facility setting gives it a different purpose. Pickering Barn is intended to function as a community resilience hub rather than as a merchant storage plant earning grid-market revenue. A resilience hub needs defined critical services The barn serves as an event venue and home of the Issaquah Farmers Market. During emergencies, the resilience-hub concept calls for community services such as warming, cooling, charging and other support, but the reviewed materials do not specify which electrical loads the planned battery would maintain or for how long. That missing load definition will determine whether 60 kWh is sufficient for the intended mission. HVAC, lighting, communications, refrigeration, charging and accessibility equipment can have very different power and energy requirements. The project is comparable in purpose to the planned Saint Paul Oxford Community Center microgrid, where a city is also pairing solar, storage and facility upgrades around a community lifeline function. The Issaquah project is distinct because it has selected a sodium-ion design and disclosed a 60 kWh energy target. Certification and procurement are the next decisive steps The next material milestones will be completion of the battery design, certification results, city procurement and permit approvals, installation and tests showing that the system can transition safely into islanded operation. Commissioning should verify more than whether the battery charges. artigo.texto: Your RAM Has Entered the Chat Your computer probably did not expect to become a supporting character in the AI infrastructure debate. Yet here we are. Sam Altman has questioned whether scarce memory belongs in personal machines when shared servers could put it to work more often. The OpenAI chief made the argument on Cheeky Pint, the podcast hosted by Stripe cofounder John Collison. The episode carries an October 29, 2026 publication date. The Verge subsequently highlighted the remark in its reporting. It is an attention-grabbing position. People buy computer memory to make their own machines useful. AI companies buy memory to serve enormous numbers of customers. Both groups have perfectly understandable reasons to want more. Altman’s statement throws those interests into the same shopping basket. Unfortunately, the basket contains limited silicon, competing priorities, and enough friction to power a small comment section. What Altman Actually Argued The important context is local inference: running an AI model on your own device rather than sending requests to a remote service. Altman challenged the assumption that distributing models across personal computers automatically solves infrastructure constraints. His concern centered on utilization. Memory installed in individual machines may spend much of its life waiting. A shared cloud system can potentially spread work across many customers and keep expensive resources busier. Altman called the allocation “quite terrible” and said people’s memory might be used “5% of the time.” He favored “maximum utilization in the cloud.” Those phrases explain the controversy. However, the exchange supplied no supporting study for that percentage. Readers should treat it as Altman’s assertion, rather than a measured average covering every desktop, laptop, workload, and household. That distinction matters. A memorable number can become accepted fact surprisingly quickly once headlines start passing it around. The Strongest Case for Sharing Consider a hypothetical office with ten employees who each need a powerful tool for a short, different period. Buying ten copies guarantees immediate access. Sharing fewer copies could meet the same demand with less equipment, provided the schedules cooperate. Cloud computing applies a version of that logic to computing resources. Pooling demand can reduce the amount of capacity that sits unused between jobs. This is the strongest interpretation of Altman’s argument. Under tight supply, hardware that serves more useful requests may deliver more benefit per unit of memory. But the conditions do heavy lifting. Requests must fit the available hardware. Customers must tolerate the service’s response time. Peak demand must remain manageable. Sharing works beautifully until everyone wants the office printer at once. Then the elegant allocation strategy becomes a queue, and somebody starts muttering near the paper tray. Efficiency Needs a Clear Definition The analysis gets more interesting when we ask what counts as efficient. Maximum activity is one measure. Useful work completed, money spent, response time, and control over sensitive information are others. Imagine a freelance editor who needs a local tool for one urgent assignment every evening. The hardware might remain idle all afternoon. Its value still depends on being ready when the deadline arrives. That example does not disprove the advantages of pooling. It shows why utilization alone cannot settle every purchasing decision. We do not usually judge a fire extinguisher by how many hours it spends spraying foam. Availability can have value even when a resource waits. Computers are different from emergency equipment, of course. Still, the broader principle holds: a lower activity rate does not automatically establish that an owner bought something wasteful or that centralized access would serve them better. Why the Memory Market Matters This debate has a physical foundation. AI software depends on manufactured components, and chipmakers must decide how to allocate production across different products. Micron has explained that HBM3E, a form of high-bandwidth memory used with AI accelerators, requires roughly three times the wafer supply of DDR5 to produce the same number of bits at the same technology node. That comparison helps explain how AI demand can place pressure on the wider memory industry. Manufacturing more advanced AI memory can require substantial production resources. It does not mean a desktop memory stick can simply move into an AI accelerator. Different memory products have different designs, packaging, and platform requirements. The competition operates partly through manufacturing capacity and investment decisions. Think competing recipes using a constrained kitchen, rather than identical sandwiches being snatched from different lunchboxes. The distinction makes the shortage easier to understand without turning every RAM purchase into a technical misunderstanding. OpenAI Is Already at the Table Altman’s comments also land against the backdrop of OpenAI’s own infrastructure ambitions. This is a major buyer discussing the best destination for a scarce product it wants to purchase. In October 2025, OpenAI announced partnerships with Samsung and SK aimed at expanding advanced memory production and data center capacity. Its announcement identified a target of 900,000 DRAM wafer starts per month. That is a production target, not a count of finished retail memory modules. It also should not become shorthand for a proven amount already delivered. SK’s separate announcement described a memory supply letter of intent and said specific volumes and arrangements would require further discussions. These details matter because infrastructure stories often blur aspiration, agreement, construction, and operation. They represent different stages. A proposed factory cannot fill a shopping cart today, however impressive the announcement sounds. A Business Interest Wort

artigo.texto: CATL Extends Its Lead as North American Slump Weighs on Korean Manufacturers The global electric vehicle battery market continues to post double-digit growth, yet South Korean battery manufacturers are losing ground. With Chinese firms now commanding more than 70% of the global market, the combined share of South Korea’s battery makers has fallen to 12.6%, widening the gap between the two countries. According to SNE Research, an energy-focused market research firm, total battery usage in EVs, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) registered worldwide from January to September 2026 reached approximately 994.5 GWh. This represents a 19.7% increase from the same period a year earlier. Despite the market’s overall growth, the performance of Korean and Chinese firms diverged sharply. The combined market share of seven Chinese battery makers, including CATL, reached 73.0%, rising 3.5 percentage points year-on-year. In contrast, the combined share of South Korea’s three major players — LG Energy Solution, SK On and Samsung SDI — fell to 12.6%, down 4.1 percentage points from a year earlier. As a result, the market share gap between the two countries’ manufacturers widened from 52.8 percentage points to 60.4 percentage points. On a company-by-company basis, China’s CATL solidified its top position with 389.2 GWh in battery usage, a 24.9% increase year-on-year. As it expanded supply to overseas automakers, its market share rose from 37.5% to 39.1%. China’s BYD, ranked second, grew 7.4% to 150.9 GWh, though its market share declined from 16.9% to 15.2%. The combined market share of CATL and BYD stood at 54.3%, little changed from a year earlier. However, CATL's battery usage grew 17.5 percentage points faster than BYD's. Other Chinese challengers also posted strong growth, with Gotion ranking fourth, CALB fifth and EVE sixth. Among Korean firms, LG Energy Solution maintained its third-place ranking at 81.9 GWh, but its market share slipped from 9.8% to 8.2%. While usage grew in European and Asian markets, a sharp 44.9% drop in North American usage offset those gains. Its total usage increased just 0.7%, well below the overall market growth rate. SK On remained in eighth place as its total usage fell 18.1%, driven by a 46.7% decline in North American usage. Its usage totaled 28.3 GWh, and its market share fell from 4.2% to 2.8%. Regional demand disparities were equally pronounced. China’s domestic market grew 16.2%, while battery usage increased by 33.1% in Europe, 74.1% in Asia excluding China and 176.8% in South America. In contrast, the North American market contracted 24.3% year-on-year to 85.9 GWh. Korean manufacturers, which are heavily dependent on the North American market, were hit particularly hard. By battery type, the share of LFP, or lithium iron phosphate, batteries, supported by their price competitiveness, expanded from 52.5% to 57.7% over the year. South Korea’s battery industry is accelerating business diversification in response to slowing EV demand. SK On is seeking new opportunities by converting part of its Georgia plant to LFP production lines for energy storage systems (ESS) and signing a 9 GWh supply contract with a U.S.-based ESS company. LG Energy Solution and other firms are also rapidly converting their North American EV production lines for ESS use to diversify their customer base. Changes in Chinese tax policy are expected to become a key variable in the competitive landscape. China began imposing a 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries for domestic use in September 2026 and plans to eliminate value-added tax (VAT) export rebates on battery exports starting in January 2027. However, intensifying price competition among Chinese manufacturers is also weighing on profitability. SNE Research noted that CATL’s net profit growth rate in the third quarter of 2026 came in at 14.5%, far below its revenue growth rate of 58.6%. The firm said pricing strategies and the pace of customer diversification through year-end will be decisive in shaping the competitive landscape.

artigo.texto: 30MW-Class Hyperscale Facility Uses Hybrid Air Cooling, Plans Liquid Cooling, Supports 300kW+ Per Rack The first AI data center directly designed and built by a Korean company for an overseas local client has begun operations in Jakarta, Indonesia. LG CNS said on Nov. 2 that it had completed construction of a 30MW-class hyperscale AI data center in Jakarta, Indonesia. The project was ordered by KMG, a joint venture between Indonesia’s Sinar Mas Group and Korea Investment Real Asset Management, last year. The data center was designed as scalable infrastructure capable of stably supporting next-generation GPU-based high-performance computing. A key feature is its hybrid cooling structure, which combines air cooling and liquid cooling in consideration of the high heat generated by AI servers. In the first phase, an air-cooling system using an air-circulation method was applied, and in future follow-up phases the company plans to add a liquid-cooling system, which is efficient for controlling GPU heat, to provide an optimized environment. The power system was also built to withstand a high-density environment of more than 300kW per rack, about 60 times that of a typical data center rack. That level is sufficient to ensure stable power supply even for AI computing resources equipped with multiple GPUs in a single rack. In addition, the power infrastructure was built with redundancy, establishing a system capable of uninterrupted operation 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, even in emergency situations in which the main power supply is cut off. For this project, the group’s “One LG” integrated solution, centered on LG CNS’s design, build and operation (DBO) capabilities, was applied with core technologies from across the group. LG CNS is currently working on the design for a follow-up phase aimed at expanding total receiving power capacity to 400MW. Once construction is completed, the facility is expected to establish itself as one of Indonesia’s representative large-scale AI data centers. Along with this overseas expansion, LG CNS is also accelerating the diversification of its business model. In addition to its existing colocation and DBO businesses, it has been expanding its portfolio to include prefabricated modular data centers, GPUaaS that provides GPUs on a subscription basis, and liquid-cooling infrastructure. Going forward, the company plans to develop these into an “AI Factory” business linked with AI platforms and services. Hyun Shin-gyoon, CEO of LG CNS, said, "This completion is a meaningful achievement that demonstrates competitiveness in the global market by providing overseas customers with the data center capabilities accumulated in Korea," adding, "We will continue to expand our AI data center and AI Factory businesses in the global market, where demand for AI computing is surging."

artigo.texto: PAGE, Ariz. -- Doug Herrera still lives in the house his father built, though his dad died some time ago from cancer. Herrera wonders if that illness could have been linked to pollutants from nearby uranium mining. Now, he worries that a possible new neighbor -- a proposed $10 billion mega data center -- could imperil his health. "I'm a patriot, but I'm highly against the data center," Herrera, 64, said from his front porch near a yard sign that reads "No Data Centers." "There is light pollution, sound pollution. The temperature is going to rise," he said. Page is a gateway to iconic Southwestern landscapes of arid deserts studded with Joshua trees and towering red-rock formations. While the City Council approved the sale of land for a data center, the developer needs zoning and other approvals. Residents concerned about possible health effects have signed petitions and mobilized to oppose construction. The boom in data centers is dividing communities such as Page and turning future construction into a flash point in the midterm elections. The leading candidates in the close race for Arizona's 1st Congressional District are at odds over any new centers there, and the state's attorney general has called for a pause on new approvals and building. Emerging research into data centers' possible health effects is adding grist to the various state fights, giving ammunition to Democrats and some Republicans who've broken party ranks to oppose the sprawling complexes. It has also put some incumbent politicians who have supported data center expansion in unexpectedly vulnerable positions in reliably red states like Ohio and Texas, where the megabuildings now operate by the hundreds. "Two years ago, a lot of these data centers went up and there was not an organized, watchful opposition," said Lee Hannah, PhD, a political science professor at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio. "That opposition has come up in a grassroots way so quickly that decisions made a year ago by local officials or state governments to get behind a data center are suddenly career-ending," Hannah added. The hyperscale centers house infrastructure to power artificial intelligence (AI), with servers that sprawl over tens of thousands of square feet or more. The city of Page approved the sale of 500 acres for the proposed data center, though the location within that acreage hasn't been decided. The area sits on open land studded with blackbrush and native grasses near Horseshoe Bend, an iconic curve of the Colorado River that has long been popular with tourists. Data centers gobble up electricity and rely on backup gas generators during times of peak energy demand. The resulting air pollution has been linked to heart conditions, respiratory issues, and elevated cancer risks, according to a number of environmental studies. Emissions from the centers could cause nearly 1,300 deaths annually by 2030 and an annual public health burden of more than $20 billion in 2028, based on modeling led by researchers at the University of California, Riverside. Cooling components can contain what are called forever chemicals, synthetic substances that accumulate in human tissue, according to advocacy and environmental groups. And the hum and whir of generators and heating and air conditioning systems can exceed 90 decibels, which can harm hearing. Data centers are lit up for operations and security, creating light pollution that can increase the risk of chronic disease, the groups say. The megafacilities also create what are known as data heat islands, which are higher-temperature zones caused by intense energy demands. "We're just starting to see the very early edge of the wave of the research into health impacts of data centers," said Alison Steele, executive director of the Environmental Health Project, a nonprofit public health organization. "By the time we have a substantial volume of research it's going to be too late, because the decisions are being made now." A trade group for the data center industry said a review of the largest data center market -- Virginia -- found that use of backup power sources, including diesel generators, is minimal, and that existing state and federal regulations limit potential emissions or impacts. "Data centers are committed to being responsible partners where they operate," said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs at the Data Center Coalition. It Cuts Across Politics Mounting concerns about data centers are dividing candidates and pitting some GOP contenders against President Donald Trump, who supports the facilities' construction as vital for economic growth. Two in three Americans oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., according to an October Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll. Such political standoffs are happening largely in states that Trump won in 2024, where most new data center capacity has been proposed. About 1,400 data centers operate in the U.S., and an additional 2,000-plus are planned. Sixty percent of data center capacity under construction is in states Trump won by five percentage points or more, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company. Excluding Virginia, 92% is in states the president won. Hannah said the uptick in construction has put Trump's coalition at particular risk because data centers are often built in rural areas, where the president has often enjoyed insurmountable margins of support. "This is where most of the data centers go," Hannah said. "They go into red states, because Republicans are less critical of economic opportunity. If it promises jobs and money, they're all in." In Page, signs opposing construction pepper front yards. The opposition to more data centers in the state could pose political risks for GOP House candidate Jay Feely, who won his primary with an endorsement from Trump. artigo.texto: US Data Centers Hit Political Headwinds: Candidates in 21 States Back Moratoriums, Narrowing Room for Industry Expansion The US data center industry is coming under systematic pressure from electoral politics. According to tech media outlet The Information, of the 36 states holding gubernatorial elections on Nov. 3, at least one major-party candidate in 21 states has publicly backed a moratorium on data centers. In five states—Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon and Texas—candidates from both parties hold the same position; in Maine, New Mexico and New York, the pro-moratorium side leads in the latest polls; and in seven other states the races are tight. Together, these 15 states are home to more than one-third of the US population and are also the most concentrated zone of data center construction in the country. That means that regardless of Tuesday's results, the buildable space available to the data center industry will shrink materially, with upward pressure on operating costs. Projects Under Construction Directly Exposed to Policy Risk Looking at project distribution, the footprints of major tech companies overlap heavily with the states backing moratoriums. The Stargate project, a joint venture between OpenAI and Oracle, has large sites in Texas, Michigan and New Mexico; SoftBank-owned SB Energy plans to build an 8-gigawatt campus for OpenAI in Ohio; and Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia have all established operations in Texas. Data from real estate services firm CBRE shows that metro Atlanta has overtaken Northern Virginia to become the most active data center construction market in the US, and Georgia's gubernatorial race this cycle is also among the closely contested ones. The financial implications of regulatory risk have already made their way into public filings. The IPO prospectus Anthropic released last week lists state moratoriums and other restrictive measures as a major business risk, naming moves in New York and Texas, and says regulatory pressure is one reason it is expanding its international data center footprint. SB Energy and emerging cloud service provider Nscale also list similar risks in their respective filings. Three incumbent governors have already moved first: New York's Kathy Hochul, Texas's Greg Abbott and Oregon's Tina Kotek have all paused approvals for new large data center projects. Hochul's opponent, Bruce Blakeman, has called the moratorium "absurd" but trails badly in the polls; Abbott's opponent, Gina Hinojosa, describes the pause on her campaign website as an "election-year gimmick," suggesting it will lapse after Nov. 4, while advocating a broader, comprehensive moratorium. A Shift in Public Opinion Is the Root Cause The political sensitivity of data centers has risen sharply in a short period, driven by a rapid shift in public opinion. At the start of this year, about 40 towns and counties across the US had imposed bans on data centers; by August the number had surpassed 500, reflecting residents' concerns about rising electricity bills, water consumption, noise pollution and environmental damage. An August poll by the Pew Research Center found that six in ten US adults said they were unwilling to see a new data center built near their community, more than half believed data centers are harmful to the environment, and half said they drive up household electricity bills; fewer than one in four respondents believed data centers benefit local jobs or tax revenue. Association with the data center industry has become a political liability. Nevada Democrat Aaron Ford has branded Republican incumbent Governor Joe Lombardo "Data Center Joe" and set up a dedicated website to promote the label; Wisconsin Republican Tom Tiffany calls his opponent David Crowley "Data Center Dave"; and Oregon Democrats call their opponent Christine Drazan "Data Center Drazan." Alabama's popular candidate Tommy Tuberville, previously a strong industry backer, dismissed such concerns as "nonsense" in July; his campaign ads now strike a different tone: "Politicians grab the headlines, Big Tech takes the tax breaks, and ordinary families foot the bill." Moratoriums Vary Widely in Substance The term "moratorium" is ubiquitous in political discourse, but the substance of policies varies widely by location. On duration, some pauses last just 45 days while others run as long as three years, with most intended to buy time for legislatures to set longer-term standards. On scope, some moratoriums target only facilities above a certain size—New York sets a 50-megawatt threshold, rejecting large campuses used to train frontier AI models but allowing smaller projects to proceed; the "conditional moratorium" backed by Ohio candidate Amy Acton stipulates that data centers meeting certain labor and siting conditions may still be approved. The enforcement mechanism, by contrast, is highly consistent: moratoriums already implemented in the states all rely on halting new environmental permit approvals, with Abbott additionally freezing new grid connection applications and Kotek suspending related transactions on state-owned land. New Hampshire's incumbent governor, Kelly Ayotte, says she cannot act alone and needs to advance the measure through the state budget process next July; her opponent, Cinde Warmington, has pledged to sign an executive order on her first day in office. Not all candidates have chosen the moratorium path. Of the 46 major candidates who have not called for a pause, 38 support at least one restrictive measure targeting data centers, including electricity bill protections, eliminating tax breaks, tougher environmental and water-use requirements, mandatory union labor, and bans on confidentiality agreements in public transactions. Hawaii is the only state where neither party's candidate has proposed data center restrictions. artigo.texto: South Korean AI Data Center Industry Urges Government to Set Up Dedicated Power-Supply Desk With uncertainty over power supply cited as the biggest obstacle to AI data center investment, the industry is calling on the government to establish a dedicated desk and to set clear deadlines for permit processing. Companies say that because they cannot know when or how much electricity they will receive while still reviewing a site, decisions to buy land or commit capital are being held up. The Federation of Korean Industries (FKI) on the 2nd jointly hosted a corporate roundtable on "Revitalizing the AI Data Center Industry Ecosystem" with South Korea's Presidential Committee on AI at the FKI Tower in Yeouido, Seoul. Fifteen companies attended, including Samsung SDS, Hyundai Motor, LG Electronics, FuriosaAI, Rebellions and HyperExcel, to discuss policy improvements needed to boost investment and foster related industries. Power emerged as the most urgent issue. Data center companies asked for a channel through which they can consult relevant agencies on the timing and capacity of power supply even before a site is finalized. The permitting process, split across building, transportation, environment and electrical equipment approvals, was also flagged for improvement, since a delay in any single procedure can push back the entire completion schedule and inflate project costs. The industry recommended that the subordinate regulations of the Special Act on the Promotion of the AI Data Center Industry, set to take effect next March, specify permit processing deadlines and establish a system that coordinates consultations among agencies. Attendees also proposed supplying locally generated renewable energy directly to nearby data centers. Regions with concentrated renewable generation, such as South Korea's southwestern region, often cannot use all the power they produce because of insufficient grid capacity. The industry suggested using microgrids — small-scale power networks combining on-site generation with energy storage systems (ESS) — as an alternative. Companies asked for special provisions and institutional support so that demonstration projects under way at industrial complexes and universities in South Jeolla Province can be expanded into power supply for data centers. South Korean AI chipmakers said they need opportunities to validate their products in actual data centers and build a supply track record. They explained that neural processing units (NPUs) with improved computational efficiency and power consumption have reached the commercialization stage, but compatibility issues with existing software built around foreign graphics processing units (GPUs) are blocking adoption. Public procurement practices were also cited as a problem. Some public AI projects are ordered on the premise of specific GPU products or server configurations, which can narrow the room for South Korean NPUs to participate, according to the companies. They asked that procurement criteria be changed to focus on the performance and capacity needed for actual services such as training and inference. Power and cooling equipment makers said that even when they develop next-generation products, a lack of testing opportunities and data center deployment records makes it hard to enter the market. Operators, for their part, must bear the cost and operational risk of adopting equipment with few proven cases. The industry recommended building large-scale testing facilities, subsidizing the cost of participating in demonstrations, and simplifying the review process for the Korea Certification (KC) integrated national mark. Ha Jung-woo, vice chair of South Korea's Presidential Committee on AI, stressed that AI data centers are an industry that brings together semiconductors, power, cooling and networking technologies, and that South Korean companies' capabilities must be pooled. "Our companies need to connect and advance these technologies well and grow them into high-value 'token factories' that will become a new growth engine for our economy," he said. "Token factory" is a term likening AI data centers to factories that take in power, semiconductors and data and produce everything from text, images and code to the intelligence used to control manufacturing equipment and robots. Kim Chang-beom, senior executive vice chairman of the FKI, said, "It is now important not only how many AI data centers we build but what we fill them with." He added, "We need to create a virtuous cycle in which our companies' semiconductor, power and cooling technologies are used in South Korean data centers, and that experience leads to global orders and exports." The roundtable was organized around the recognition that regulatory uncertainty must be cleared away first if AI infrastructure investment is to translate into South Korean industrial competitiveness. With subordinate regulations being drafted ahead of the special law's implementation, attention is focused on whether the industry's proposals will be reflected in the actual rules. Waiting times for grid connections and permitting delays are cited as common bottlenecks in global data center investment as well. In South Korea too, large-scale private investment could be postponed unless power supply schedules are fixed, which would in turn affect the pace of expanding AI service infrastructure. In semiconductors and equipment, attendees highlighted that South Korean data centers can serve as the first proving ground for South Korean-made products, since companies that secure early references can gain an edge in winning orders abroad. South Korea's Presidential Committee on AI and the FKI plan to flesh out the proposals raised at the meeting and continue consultations so they can be reflected in the government's AI strategy and related policies.

artigo.texto: Gia Lai prepara-se para inaugurar um mercado de créditos de carbono. O Comitê Popular da província de Gia Lai acaba de aprovar um plano abrangente para o desenvolvimento de um mercado de créditos de carbono, visando explorar o valor de mais de 1 milhão de hectares de florestas e ecossistemas, criando uma nova fonte de financiamento para servir à proteção ambiental, à adaptação às mudanças climáticas e à meta de emissões líquidas zero até 2050. De acordo com o plano, de agora até 2028, a província construirá um banco de dados de carbono, um sistema de medição, relato e verificação (MRV) e implementará de um a três projetos-piloto sobre carbono florestal, carbono da pesca, conservação marinha e redução de emissões do transporte público de ônibus. Durante o período de 2029 a 2030, Gia Lai se empenhará para que os créditos de carbono florestal sejam incluídos no mercado interno, de acordo com o roteiro nacional. A província almeja ter 20.000 hectares de terras cultivadas com emissões reduzidas, coletar e reutilizar 100% dos resíduos pecuários em grandes fazendas e ter pelo menos 30% dos ônibus movidos a energia verde. Até 2050, a província pretende formar um ecossistema de carbono transparente e intimamente conectado ao mercado internacional. Você também pode gostar Gia Lai tem a vantagem de uma área natural de mais de 21.500 km², com mais de 1,03 milhão de hectares de floresta e terras destinadas ao reflorestamento, e uma taxa de cobertura florestal de quase 46%. Desse total, cerca de 692.000 hectares de floresta natural servem como base para a implementação do mecanismo de redução de emissões REDD+, e mais de 294.000 hectares de floresta plantada contribuem para o aumento dos estoques de carbono. Além da silvicultura, Gia Lai também explora o potencial de redução de emissões em quase 977.000 hectares de terras agrícolas com culturas importantes como café, seringueira, pimenta, mandioca e cana-de-açúcar. As soluções propostas incluem o cultivo de arroz com baixas emissões, a expansão da agricultura regenerativa, o controle dos gases de efeito estufa na pecuária em larga escala, o desenvolvimento de energias renováveis e a criação de ecossistemas de carbono verde em áreas costeiras e lagunares. Você também pode gostar De acordo com o plano, o valor dos recursos naturais será gradualmente transformado em ativos ambientais negociáveis. A receita legítima proveniente dos créditos de carbono será gerida de forma transparente, priorizando o reinvestimento na proteção ambiental, na adaptação às mudanças climáticas e na melhoria dos meios de subsistência sustentáveis para as pessoas.

artigo.texto: Among the nearly 100 pages of risk factors outlined in Anthropic PBC’s landmark initial public offering are the catastrophic threats to humanity that have grabbed headlines. However, it also flagged a more immediate concern that could derail business: mounting backlash against data centers. Public controversy and regulatory scrutiny over the environmental impact, land and water use as well as consumption of limited power resources threaten to delay or prevent data-center development, Anthropic said in the prospectus. That would raise costs and limit its ability to scale, develop and deploy artificial intelligence (AI) models, it says. The company is right to worry. Hatred toward data centers has united people across the political spectrum and around the globe. Warning that the technology could create existential risks probably does not inspire anyone to want to give the AI boom a physical address in their backyards. Illustration: Yusha Opposition to the build-out has surfaced in Australia, the UK and even rural China. Now, it is starting to fester in pockets of Japan, just as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is pushing massive investment. Meanwhile, Anthropic is reportedly in final talks with NTT Data Group to build one of the country’s biggest data centers near Osaka. Yet while anxiety around the technology runs high globally, the Japanese are unusually sanguine about it — robots are seen here more as friendly helpers such as Doraemon than The Terminator. For a smaller, relatively insular economy facing acute labor shortages and demographic pressures, the upsides could be enormous. Many of AI’s strengths neatly address Japan’s acute gaps: translation in a country that has been flooded with foreign tourists, software engineering in a tech industry historically stronger in hardware than coding, boosting efficiency for small and medium-size manufacturers, and easing administrative burdens for the growing cohort of elder caregivers. The list goes on. For now, Japan’s opposition is scattered and local, hardly close to the organized political movement we are seeing in the US. However, there was little excuse anywhere to be so caught off guard. I have been tracking the AI backlash for a while, and the industry’s implicit threat that this might kill us all or take your job has never been an effective way to greet new neighbors. Outside of the Silicon Valley bubble, data centers as the physical manifestation of an abstract tech revolution have become easy targets. It is more than noise, eyesore or water use. It is about having a say. This is partly why the US revolt goes far beyond NIMBYism. Nearly three-quarters of Americans oppose having a data center in their community, while two-thirds are against new ones anywhere. It is already having a material impact: In the first half of this year alone, at least 106 projects, representing about US$198 billion in investment, were blocked or delayed, the Data Center Watch said. It offers lessons for Tokyo to not assume these are just isolated groups of Luddites. Japan has the most favorable environment for data center development among the OECD markets in the Asia-Pacific region, given its established digital infrastructure sector, BloombergNEF assessed. It already has some 2 gigawatts of operating IT capacity, second in the region only to China. Local opposition is a lurking threat, but the more immediate constraint is power. These facilities guzzle enormous amounts of energy to run servers and cooling, and Japan has never been energy rich. Power demand from new data centers and chip fabs is expected to rise from less than 1 percent of the country’s electricity consumption this year to nearly 7 percent by 2035, SMBC Nikko analysts have said. Addressing this challenge could help catalyze a broader shift toward clean energy. The government, for its part, seems aware of the problem. Takaichi has pledged a “sufficient and stable supply of electricity” to meet the growing demands from data centers, doubling down on an earlier promise to “take all possible measures” to do so. The policy direction is right, if ambitious, but increasing investments in green energy would help Japan build resilience in the future, not just power these facilities. Currently, most data center capacity is concentrated in the Greater Tokyo region and Osaka. Mindful of risks in the event of earthquakes or other unexpected shocks, officials have identified potential future sites in Hokkaido, Kyushu and elsewhere. Spreading infrastructure beyond crowded urban areas would also reduce some of the nuisance complaints that have fueled opposition elsewhere. Japan was initially slow to adopt AI, but usage has finally surged. That delay could become a second-mover advantage that the country cannot afford to squander as investors start questioning the payoff from the expensive, hype-fueled AI infrastructure spree. The country has long excelled at developing infrastructure that works for people, from trains that run on time to urban design that fosters community. That could be a major advantage. If Tokyo can construct data centers without neighbors bringing out the pitchforks, it could define what comes next. Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners. artigo.texto: Dear Editor, As a parent and a teacher, I urge local leaders to demand accountability for data centers. Right now, big polluters are profiting while our families foot the bill. Data centers take up acres of much-needed land that could otherwise be used for affordable housing, education or agriculture. We need our rural landscapes to keep protecting wildlife and providing clean air and water. READ MORE The rush to power data centers is driving new fossil fuel development, threatening climate progress and bringing more toxic pollution to communities. Instead, we could be powering our lives with clean energy that protects our wallets, our climate and our health. The progress we have made in the last 20 years in restricting emissions and reducing pollution will be reversed, especially if data centers are gas powered. This shouldn’t be a difficult choice. Let’s hold data centers accountable with common-sense guardrails now. Anne D’Olivo Manchester, Vt.
