artigo.texto: A Google energy executive has told reporters that data centers in orbit can cost up to 100 times more than the same capacity on the ground, according to a report from The Information. We could not open the original paywalled story, so the executive’s name, the exact wording and the method behind the 100x figure remain unconfirmed in this article. What we can verify is the surrounding picture: Google’s own researchers, outside engineers and rival space firms all agree that orbital computing costs more than terrestrial computing today, and they disagree mainly on how much more. The timing matters. Google launched its first Project Suncatcher test satellite on Oct. 1, 2026, and the spacecraft started answering prompts within weeks. We covered that milestone when the first orbital TPU replied with a haiku. Now the company’s own energy leadership is putting a hard price warning on the idea, just as investors weigh a record wave of earthbound data center spending. This analysis lays out what is known about the claim, how it compares with other published estimates, why launch economics dominate the math, and what the number means for cloud buyers who plan capacity over the next five years. It also offers five predictions and a short FAQ. Throughout, we attribute figures to the outlet that published them and label our own arithmetic as arithmetic. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Google’s Energy Chief Reportedly Said About Space Data Centers The headline claim is simple. An energy chief at Google said space data centers can cost up to 100 times more than data centers on Earth, and The Information carried the story. The phrase “up to” matters. It signals a ceiling for the worst case rather than a central estimate, and it likely reflects a spread of scenarios that depend on launch price, satellite lifetime and how much compute each satellite carries. We searched for the underlying text and found no public version of it. Searches for the 100x phrase surfaced only unrelated uses of the number, such as one startup’s plan to give its second spacecraft 100 times the power generation of its first. That absence does not make the claim false. Paywalled scoops often circulate for days before other outlets match the details. It does mean readers should treat the multiplier as reported rather than independently confirmed. One more caution applies. A cost multiplier on its own says little without a baseline. A 100x premium over a cheap grid-connected hall in Iowa is a different statement from a 100x premium over a 2030 gigawatt campus with its own nuclear supply. Until the original report’s assumptions surface, the safest reading is directional: Google’s energy side sees orbital compute as far more expensive than the ground option for now. How 100x Compares With Other Published Estimates The 100x figure sits at the extreme end of a wide range. IEEE Spectrum estimated that designing, building and launching a one-gigawatt orbital data center would cost more than $50 billion, based on a network of about 4,300 satellites and including five years of operating costs. The same analysis put a comparable terrestrial facility at roughly $16 billion. That is a premium of about three times, not one hundred. Skeptics quoted in 2026 coverage land in the same neighborhood. A roundup of the sector reported that critics calculate orbital compute at roughly three times the cost per watt of ground equivalents. Proponents argue the opposite direction. Starcloud, a startup that already flew an Nvidia H100 in orbit, claims unit economics near $0.05 per kilowatt-hour that would make orbital capacity competitive with terrestrial power by the early 2030s. Elon Musk has said space-based solar data centers could beat ground ones within two to three years, a timeline that CNBC’s June 2026 analysis called disputed. Read together, the table shows a spread of two orders of magnitude, from parity to 100x. The spread exists because each party picks a different launch price, hardware life and workload. That makes the 100x figure less a rebuttal of Google’s own research than a different slice of the same model, run with pessimistic inputs. Why Launch Cost Drives the Gap Nearly every serious analysis starts with price per kilogram to low Earth orbit. Google’s researchers argued that orbital computing approaches parity with ground data centers on a cost-per-kilowatt basis once launch falls to about $200 per kilogram. Coverage of the original Suncatcher research put today’s Falcon Heavy price near $1,500 per kilogram, and projected a drop toward $200 by around 2035. Other published ranges run from about $1,000 to $2,900 per kilogram depending on vehicle and customer, and one 2026 sector roundup cited about $2,700 per kilogram for Falcon 9. Simple division shows how sensitive the result is. At $2,700 per kilogram, launch costs run 13.5 times the $200 target. At $1,500 they run 7.5 times. Launch is only one line item, because hardened chips, solar arrays, radiators, inter-satellite links and replacement flights add cost on top. A pessimistic stack of those items is how an analyst could reach a very high multiple. Back-of-envelope arithmetic (ours, not a forecast) Launch price vs. Google's $200/kg parity target $2,700 / $200 = 13.5x $1,500 / $200 = 7.5x Capacity cost for a 1 GW site, using IEEE Spectrum's terrestrial baseline $16B x 3 = $48B (close to IEEE Spectrum's "over $50B") $16B x 100 = $1.6T (what a literal 100x would imply) The $1.6 trillion line is the useful sanity check. No credible developer plans a gigawatt of orbital capacity at that price, so a literal 100x would describe a scenario nobody intends to build. It is a warning about what happens if launch prices stay flat and satellites fail early, not a quote for a project. Launch supply is the second constraint. Quilty Space analysts have warned the industry may fall about 150 launches short

artigo.texto: A lawsuit seeking to reverse the Sangamon County Board’s April 7 approval of zoning to allow for construction of a data center could hinge on the court’s interpretation of the word “shall” within the county’s data center code. Circuit Judge Adam Giganti, at the conclusion of an Oct. 30 hearing on motions to dismiss the suit, said he’s “going to take the matter under advisement and will render a decision as soon as possible.” The July 6 lawsuit was originally filed against Sangamon County and the County Board by residents who live approximately a mile or less from the site. They are seeking to overturn the county’s approval of the project, claiming procedural violations and unchecked environmental concerns. The Sangamon County Board approved a conditional use permit on April 7 that would allow a data center to be constructed on 280 acres of farmland by a vote of 17-10, with one board member abstaining. Amongst other things such as lack of a noise study and pollution concerns, the suit claims the approved zoning petition had insufficient documentation as required by the County Code’s own language stating “(t)he petition for a conditional permitted use for a data center shall include… letters from the serving utility companies indicating the availability and adequacy of utility services.” The County Board approved the zoning petition despite the electricity utility letter submitted referencing a different data center project altogether and the water utility letter stating it was still reviewing CyrusOne’s application. The County Board’s lawyers argue that the Board was “conditionally approving the (conditional use) permit contingent on future submission of these materials.” The Rural Electric Convenience Cooperative will-serve electricity letter, dated Aug. 26, 2025, makes no mention of CyrusOne but it does say the electric co-op will provide electricity to a different, substantially smaller project called the Diamond Core Data Center. The Jan. 29 Apple Creek Water Cooperative letter included in the zoning petition states the water utility is still reviewing CyrusOne’s application. READ PREVIOUS ILLINOIS TIMES COVERAGE OF THE LAWSUIT HERE: Data center lawsuit could be tossed out County Board defends data center approval in court Residents sue Sangamon County, CyrusOne Illinois Times called and emailed both utility companies and Sean Middleton, president and CEO of RECC – who has been publicly supportive of the project – over the past three weeks asking if either company could provide updated will-serve utility letters for the CyrusOne data center project but neither responded to numerous requests. Apple Creek Water Cooperative referred Illinois Times to its attorney from Rammelkamp Bradney but multiple voicemails left for Bradley Wilson were not returned. In court, the county’s lawyers from Champaign law firm Webber & Thies argued the plaintiffs’ “artful pleading” is because the residents are simply upset with the outcome of April’s vote. The lawyers say the county had plenty of reason for approving the data center through the potential for economic incentives, so the lawsuit should be terminated. “The County Board here or the legislature or whatever legislative body it is has policy power. They have the right to legislate. They are making decisions. They are the people’s representatives. The ordinary citizen’s remedy – if they disagree with that decision – is political,” said attorney Daniel Thies during the Oct. 30 hearing. “We don’t want ordinary citizens who have lost in the political process to be able then to hold out the legislators. “The county’s legislative body can decide that it’s going to value economic development more than the potential for a little bit of pollution. That is a prerogative of the people’s representatives through their elected body,” Thies said. The county’s own staff report shows about $71 million of projected property tax revenue would go to three taxing bodies based in Macoupin County, with six Sangamon-based taxing districts expected to split roughly $27 million over a 20-year period, if all assessments go according to plan. Sangamon County itself could expect to see just over $445,000 for 20 years in annual tax revenue, though some large data centers in northern Illinois and other parts of the country have later appealed for property tax reductions. Meanwhile, no state or local sales tax will apply to any of the anticipated $500 million investment since CyrusOne secured a tax break before Gov. JB Pritzker’s executive order to pause a state program providing deals to developers went into effect. As for property value concerns, Thies said the existence of a data center could lead to nearby property value increases with the potential for neighboring data center developments. “There was testimony of a real estate appraiser who studied this question and determined that the surrounding property values, in fact, would not be depressed and very well could rise as they have adjacent other data centers that have been built around the country,” he said. Chloe Russell, a Plainfield lawyer representing members of the Caruthers family, who have farmed land in southwest Sangamon County for close to two centuries, and Cathy Bettis, owner of Joette Kennel, argued Oct. 30 the complaint is not contending issues with the county’s reasoning but “it pleads the county’s violations” of “mandatory petition elements. “On the utility letters, both defendants point to the conditions in the approval order requiring updated and definitive will-serve letters before a building permit is issued. Those conditions prove our point. If the letters had been adequate, no condition would have been needed,” she said, before pointing out how each will-serve letter does not comply with the county’s own code. “The ordinance says the petition ‘shall include,’ before the board acts. The statute presupposes a complete petition; it does not excuse an incomplete petition.” Northwestern University professo

artigo.texto: *This content was translated by AI.View Original As the Chinese government imposes a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries while including sodium-ion batteries in the scope of tax incentives, major battery companies such as HiNa Battery are accelerating efforts to build large-scale production systems aimed at the commercial electric vehicle market. Through an announcement issued by China’s Ministry of Finance, General Administration of Customs, and State Taxation Administration, a 2% consumption tax will be levied on specific lithium-ion batteries starting September 1 this year, with plans to raise the rate to 4% in the future. In contrast, sodium-ion batteries, all-solid-state batteries, and fuel cells are exempt from the consumption tax until December 31, 2028, provided they meet national standards. Such tax benefits serve as policy support to offset the narrowing price competitiveness of sodium batteries due to falling lithium prices. Against this policy backdrop, HiNa Battery signed an agreement to build a sodium-ion battery production base with an annual capacity of 10 GWh in Jiangxia District, Wuhan City. As the first phase, a 3 GWh facility will be constructed first, with construction set to begin in early 2027 and initial production to commence within that year. In addition, HiNa Battery is partnering with Qingli Special Vehicle Group to develop sodium-battery-based special-purpose sanitation vehicles, including street sweepers and food waste collection trucks. Sodium-ion batteries are noted for their excellent low-temperature performance as a key strength. Tests on large commercial vehicles demonstrated that they maintain over 90% of available capacity even in extreme environments at minus 40 degrees Celsius. However, challenges remain, including limits in energy density and the manufacturing process for hard-carbon anode materials, so initial adoption is expected to be active primarily among large commercial vehicles and special-purpose vehicles rather than passenger cars. *This content was translated by AI.View Original

artigo.texto: SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI, lost its bid to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit, which is proceeding in federal court in Mississippi, according to a judge's opinion released late Friday. The lawsuit claims that the AI division of CEO Elon Musk's aerospace and defense tech conglomerate violated the Clean Air Act with its use of gas-fired combustion turbines to power its massive AI data centers in Greater Memphis. The Colossus data centers and a power plant that SpaceXAI is also building in Southaven, Mississippi, have faced community backlash for years. The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice filed the suit on behalf of the NAACP in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi in April 2026. The suit alleges that between August and December 2025, xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech, installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, "without an air permit or regard for the health and safety of people living nearby." (SpaceXAI is owned and operated by SpaceX, which has rebranded it as SpaceXAI or SpaceXSI.) The turbines emit smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that can increase health risks and cause an unpleasant odor, among other unwanted impacts, according to the suit. Lawyers for SpaceXAI argued in their motion to dismiss, filed in June, that the NAACP suit should be tossed because the company's use of the turbines, which it characterized as "mobile," was exempt from permitting requirements. They also argued that NAACP didn't have a right to sue under the federal Clean Air Act, and suits by such community groups were unconstitutional. The judge presiding over the case rejected those arguments, writing: "Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs' claims will proceed." The decision comes about two weeks after the same court rejected a Department of Justice's request to end the case against Musk's company. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

artigo.texto: Bess Atwell announces new album Cut A Figure Bess Atwell announces her new album Cut A Figure, arriving February 5th via Nettwerk. Ahead of the LP’S arrival, the artist has shared new single “Glass” accompanied by a new video and confirmed live dates. For her 2024 Aaron Dessner-produced album Light Sleeper, Bess Atwell retreated from the UK to Quebec, where she lived for nine months, writing what would become Cut a Figure. To bring the album to life, she worked with Los Angeles-based producer and mixer Chris Coady (Beach House, Future Islands, DIIV, Foals, and more). Atwell explains, “I knew I wanted to name the album after a line in this song as it feels like the heart of the record. Sometimes, an eagerness to be seen and understood can have the opposite effect – you can be so transparent that you end up invisible. When I was a teenager, I was really into doing ‘personality tests’. One test had you imagine a cube and then describe it (the cube supposedly representing how you express yourself). All my friends and family pictured various different sizes and colors, while I saw a transparent glass box floating in space.” Bess Atwell Cut A Figure Nettwerk Records Tracklisting To Disappear Two of Wands I Was A Mirror End in Tears Glass Strike One The Act Tonight I Am Allowed What Did We Eat Out for Eleven Your Name Bess Atwell 2027 Tour Dates January 28th, Tramway, Glasgow January 31st, The Crossing, Birmingham February 6th, The Barbican, London – Album launch show North America March 2nd, L’Esco, Montreal March 3rd, Rainbow, Ottawa March 4th, Horseshoe Tavern, Toronto March 6th, 939 Cafe, Boston March 7th, Elsewhere, New York March 8th, Johnny Brenda’s, Philadelphia March 10th, Schubas, Chicago March 12th, Conor Byrne Pub, Seattle March 13th, Wise Hall, Vancouver March 14th, Show Bar, Portland March 16th, Rickshaw Stop, San Francisco March 18th, Moroccan Lounge, Los Angeles Australia March 24th, Oxford Art Factory, Sydney March 25th, Corner Hotel, Melbourne March 27th, Brightside, Brisbane March 30th, Jive Bar, Adelaide UK & Ireland April 20th, Future Yard, Birkenhead April 21st, Irish Centre, Leeds April 22nd, Glasshouse International Centre For Music, Gateshead April 23rd, New Century Hall, Manchester April 25th, Limelight 2, Belfast April 27th, Whelan’s, Dublin April 29th, Rescue Rooms, Nottingham April 30th, Electric, Bristol Europe May 18th, La Boule Noire, Paris May 19th, Ekko, Utrecht May 20th, Hebebühne, Hamburg May 21st, Privatclub, Berlin May 23rd, Ideal Bar, Copenhagen pre order Cut A Figure by Bess Atwell HERE Advertisement Join the Northern Transmissions insiders list Sign up for reviews, interviews, news, videos, playlists — and more.

artigo.texto: Nvidia pode garantir dívida bilionária de data center de IA Fabricante de chips estuda ser fiadora de empréstimos da Nscale para construção de campus de IA na Virgínia Ocidental, num sinal de como o setor força limites para manter a expansão. A Nvidia está negociando um papel incomum para uma fabricante de chips: o de fiadora bilionária. A empresa discute garantir parte do financiamento de dívida que a Nscale, provedora de nuvem especializada em inteligência artificial, precisa para erguer um megacampus de data centers na Virgínia Ocidental. O projeto tem como principal cliente a Anthropic, dona do chatbot Claude, que assinou um contrato de 44,6 bilhões de dólares apenas para o primeiro prédio do complexo. O arranjo, conhecido como garantia de valor residual, funcionaria assim: se a Nscale deixar de pagar os custos de construção, a Nvidia assumiria temporariamente a instalação, buscando um comprador e um novo inquilino. Não é um investimento direto. É, na prática, colocar o nome e o balanço da maior empresa de semicondutores do mundo como rede de segurança de um projeto alheio. Por que a Nvidia está disposta a ser fiadora A resposta curta é demanda. O campus da Virgínia Ocidental deve usar os chips de próxima geração Vera Rubin da Nvidia. Há ainda negociações para um segundo prédio, avaliado em cerca de 45 bilhões de dólares. Manter a Nscale de pé significa manter um canal de escoamento para centenas de milhares de GPUs de última geração. A Anthropic é uma das maiores compradoras de poder computacional do planeta. Como analisamos na cobertura do setor de IA, empresas desse porte distribuem seus gastos de infraestrutura entre vários fornecedores de chips. Para a Nvidia, garantir que o projeto da Nscale saia do papel é, indiretamente, garantir que a Anthropic continue dependente de sua arquitetura. A Nvidia já investiu cerca de 170 bilhões de dólares em aportes e linhas de crédito para neoclouds e grandes clientes. Em setembro, comprometeu 1 bilhão de dólares em financiamento conversível à própria Nscale. A diferença agora é o nível de comprometimento: até então, o apoio da fabricante cobria aluguéis e compra de chips, não obras de construção civil. O problema estrutural das neoclouds Neoclouds são provedoras de computação em nuvem focadas em IA que não contam com um negócio gerador de caixa robusto por trás. Diferente de Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure) ou Google Cloud, que financiam seus data centers com receitas de operações diversificadas, empresas como Nscale, CoreWeave e Nebius dependem quase inteiramente de captação externa. O mercado já sinalizou desconforto com esse modelo. Ações da CoreWeave, Nebius e IREN acumularam quedas superiores a 30% ao longo de outubro. A própria Nscale busca abrir capital com valuation de até 35 bilhões de dólares, mas os números operacionais são modestos: em agosto, a empresa tinha cerca de 25 mil chips avançados em operação, uma fração dos quase 500 mil que planeja implantar. Os obstáculos não são apenas financeiros. O campus na Virgínia Ocidental enfrentou problemas ambientais, com escoamento do canteiro de obras inundando residências vizinhas mais de uma vez. A certificação estadual só saiu em setembro, após meses de negociação. E neste mês, a Microsoft desistiu de um projeto da Nscale na Inglaterra depois que a conexão à rede elétrica foi empurrada para a década de 2030. Anthropic também enfrenta seus próprios desafios Do outro lado da mesa, a Anthropic não está em posição confortável. A empresa protocolou pedido de IPO, mas a Blackstone alertou investidores de que a companhia pode receber uma classificação de crédito abaixo do grau de investimento após a abertura de capital. Uma nota “junk” elevaria os custos de captação e poderia obrigar a Anthropic a continuar dependendo de parceiros financeiramente mais sólidos para lastrear suas dívidas. Esse contexto explica por que a Nvidia se dispõe a ir tão longe. Se a Anthropic tiver dificuldade para financiar sua própria expansão, ela precisa de parceiros de infraestrutura que consigam levantar capital. Se esses parceiros também não conseguem, a cadeia inteira emperra. E quem mais perde com um freio na construção de data centers é justamente quem vende os chips que vão dentro deles. Como discutimos na análise sobre o papel da Nvidia no ecossistema de IA, a empresa vem assumindo uma função que vai muito além de fabricar semicondutores. Ela atua como banco, fiadora e investidora estratégica de toda uma cadeia produtiva. É um modelo sem precedente claro na indústria de tecnologia. O que isso significa para o mercado de IA O movimento revela uma tensão estrutural no boom de inteligência artificial. Há apetite quase ilimitado por capacidade computacional, mas o financiamento dessa infraestrutura depende de modelos cada vez mais criativos e arriscados. Quando o maior fabricante de chips precisa co-assinar empréstimos de construção civil para garantir que seus produtos tenham onde ser instalados, o ecossistema está operando nos limites do viável. Para investidores, o sinal é duplo. Por um lado, confirma que a demanda por chips de IA permanece forte o suficiente para justificar compromissos bilionários. Por outro, mostra que o elo mais frágil da cadeia não é a tecnologia, mas a infraestrutura física e seu financiamento. Como acompanhamos na editoria de finanças, setores que dependem de alavancagem pesada em ambientes de juros elevados tendem a sofrer correções abruptas quando a confiança dos credores oscila. A decisão final da Nvidia sobre a garantia ainda não foi formalizada. Mas o simples fato de a negociação existir já diz muito sobre o estágio em que o ciclo de investimento em IA se encontra: a fase em que construir é tão difícil quanto inventar. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentabilidade passada não é garantia de resultados futuros.

artigo.texto: BYD is moving upmarket with its new flagship EV, featuring suicide doors, a gemstone grille, and possibly solid-state batteries. BYD previews Yangwang Altior suicide doors and grille Yangwang is like BMW’s Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Maybach, sitting at the very top of BYD’s brand hierarchy. The ultra-luxury brand offers BYD’s most high-end and technically advanced vehicles, including the U7 sedan, the U8, a hardcore off-road SUV, and the U9, an electric supercar. Yangwang vehicles have previously debuted with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including its quad-motor e4 platform (delivering over 1,300 hp), its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its DiSus-X intelligent body control system. Its next model will push further into the elite segment. After BYD revealed the name of its new flagship executive sedan earlier this week, the Yangwang Altior, the company has released several new details ahead of its official debut. Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing confirmed on Friday that the new Yangwang Altior will feature suicide doors, a first for a BYD model. The new door design swings open nearly 90 degrees, Hu said, creating a dramatic, wide-open entrance. Hu also posted a preview of the vehicle’s front fascia, complete with a dot-matrix Gemstrone grille and crystal-inspired headlights. BYD has not confirmed many details, but the ultra-luxury sedan is expected to be about 5,500 mm (216″) in length. Images of the disguised vehicle released last month show a similar shape and size to the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom. HU said last week that the global launch of the new flagship sedan will take place in the UAE, not in BYD’s home market of China. BYD has not revealed an official date, but according to CarNewsChina, citing “sources familiar with the project,” BYD aims to unveil the new flagship model in Dubai, UAE, around November 5. The Yangwang Altrio will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said. In one image, the vehicle was charging at a BYD Flash Charge station, suggesting it will use its Blade Battery 2.0 and 5-minute Flash Charging technology. Top comment by Andrea There are companies showcasing flying cars designed specifically for circus-style shows, while others are launching solid-state batteries that can recharge in five minutes. I find myself wondering—though perhaps not too deeply—which of these technologies will secure the largest customer base and generate the greatest returns for shareholders. Outside of the suicide doors, rumors suggest the flagship model will be BYD’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries. Executive vice president Stella Li said during an interview with Carwow.es last month that BYD’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027. The executive sedan is expected to debut around November 5. Prices are rumored to start in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000. Yangwang’s current electric sedan, the U7, starts at 658,000 yuan ($98,000). The extended U8L, on the other hand, is the brand’s highest-priced mass-produced vehicle, starting at 1.45 million yuan ($217,000).

artigo.texto: TL;DR: A Proposta 45, medida de votação na Califórnia que promete acelerar a construção de infraestrutura considerada "essencial", pode abrir uma brecha para que desenvolvedores de data centers evitem a fiscalização pública, segundo alertas de ativistas ambientais. O que aconteceu A iniciativa de votação, conhecida como Proposta 45, foi apresentada como uma solução para agilizar a aprovação de projetos de infraestrutura considerados críticos, incluindo data centers, redes de energia e instalações de telecomunicações. O texto da proposta permite que esses empreendimentos sejam classificados como "essenciais", o que reduz a necessidade de avaliações ambientais detalhadas e de audiências públicas. Organizações de defesa ambiental apontam que a redação vaga da medida pode ser explorada por empresas de tecnologia para construir ou expandir data centers sem a devida transparência. A preocupação central é que, ao serem enquadrados como infraestrutura essencial, esses projetos escapariam de processos de licenciamento que normalmente exigem estudos de impacto ambiental, consultas à comunidade e divulgação de documentos técnicos. Até o momento, a proposta está em fase de campanha, com defensores argumentando que a rapidez na implantação de data centers é vital para a competitividade econômica da Califórnia, enquanto críticos temem que a falta de controle comprometa a qualidade do ar, o consumo de água e a gestão de resíduos eletrônicos. Como chegamos aqui A Califórnia tem sido um dos principais polos de tecnologia dos Estados Unidos, abrigando gigantes como Google, Amazon e Meta, que mantêm enormes fazendas de servidores para atender à demanda global de serviços em nuvem. Nos últimos anos, a pressão por maior capacidade de processamento levou a um aumento significativo na construção de data centers, especialmente em áreas com energia renovável abundante. Entretanto, a expansão acelerada trouxe desafios ambientais. Data centers consomem grandes quantidades de energia elétrica e água para refrigeração, além de gerar calor e ruído. Em resposta, a agência estadual de proteção ambiental (California Environmental Protection Agency) tem exigido avaliações de impacto cada vez mais rigorosas, o que, segundo alguns setores da indústria, retarda projetos e aumenta custos. Foi nesse contexto que a Proposta 45 surgiu, impulsionada por lobby de grandes corporações de tecnologia e grupos de interesse que defendem a desburocratização. A proposta foi incluída na cédula de votação como parte de um pacote de reformas voltadas para a modernização da infraestrutura estadual. Entretanto, organizações não‑governamentais, como a Sierra Club California, alertam que a definição de "infraestrutura essencial" está muito ampla e pode ser interpretada de forma a incluir projetos que, embora tecnicamente críticos, ainda geram impactos ambientais significativos. Elas pedem que a redação da medida seja revisada para garantir que avaliações ambientais não sejam suprimidas. O que vem depois Se aprovada, a Proposta 45 entrará em vigor imediatamente, permitindo que desenvolvedores de data centers solicitem autorizações simplificadas. Isso pode acelerar a construção de novos centros ou a expansão dos existentes, reduzindo o tempo de aprovação de meses para semanas. Por outro lado, a falta de auditoria pública pode dificultar a participação da sociedade civil em decisões que afetam a qualidade de vida nas comunidades vizinhas. A ausência de estudos de impacto pode ocultar riscos como: - Consumo excessivo de água em regiões já vulneráveis à escassez; - Emissão de gases de efeito estufa decorrente de fontes de energia não renováveis; - Poluição sonora e térmica que afeta residências e áreas naturais; - Descarte inadequado de componentes eletrônicos e resíduos de refrigerantes. Os críticos também apontam que a medida pode criar um precedente perigoso para outras categorias de projetos, como usinas de energia ou instalações de mineração, que poderiam ser classificadas como essenciais e, assim, escapar de processos de licenciamento. O futuro da Proposta 45 dependerá da campanha de informação nas próximas semanas. Grupos ambientalistas planejam intensificar a divulgação de documentos que demonstram os potenciais impactos, enquanto representantes da indústria de tecnologia prometem que a medida trará benefícios econômicos e de competitividade global. Para ficar no radar Para os leitores brasileiros interessados em tecnologia e sustentabilidade, a discussão em torno da Proposta 45 oferece alguns pontos de atenção: - Impacto nos serviços de nuvem. Caso a medida seja aprovada, a Califórnia pode acelerar a expansão de data centers, o que pode influenciar preços e disponibilidade de serviços de cloud computing usados por empresas brasileiras. - Precedente regulatório. Uma brecha legislativa nos EUA pode inspirar debates semelhantes em outras regiões, inclusive no Brasil, onde a regulação ambiental de data centers ainda está em fase de consolidação. - Consciência ambiental. O caso destaca a importância de equilibrar desenvolvimento tecnológico com responsabilidade ambiental – um tema que vem ganhando força em conferências como a Campus Party Brasil. Fique atento às próximas edições dos principais jornais californianos e aos comunicados das organizações ambientais. A decisão final será conhecida após a votação, prevista para o próximo ciclo eleitoral estadual. Independentemente do resultado, a Proposta 45 evidencia um dilema recorrente: como conciliar a necessidade de infraestrutura digital avançada com a preservação dos recursos naturais e a transparência pública? O debate está apenas começando, e o desfecho poderá moldar o futuro dos data centers não só nos EUA, mas também em mercados emergentes que buscam atrair investimentos em tecnologia.

artigo.texto: Lithium-ion batteries have become the backbone of electric vehicles and energy storage. But a rival chemistry built around one of the world’s most abundant elements is now becoming more and more viable. Sodium-ion batteries are entering commercial production, with major manufacturers betting they could make energy storage cheaper, more resilient, and less dependent on lithium. In February 2026, China’s CATL and automaker Changan unveiled what they described as the world’s first mass-production passenger vehicle equipped with sodium-ion batteries, with sales planned for the middle of the year. In April, CATL also signed a major agreement to supply 60 gigawatt-hours of sodium-ion batteries to energy storage company Beijing HyperStrong Technology over three years. These developments suggest sodium-ion technology is approaching a new stage. But it still faces a fundamental challenge. Lithium-ion batteries have a considerable head start in energy density, cost, and manufacturing scale. Sodium is abundant, but that doesn’t automatically make better batteries Both technologies work on the same basic principle. During charging and discharging, ions move between a positive electrode (cathode) and a negative electrode (anode), with an electrolyte allowing them to travel between the two. The main difference is the element carrying the charge. Lithium-ion batteries use lithium, while sodium-ion batteries use sodium, which is widely available in seawater and common salts. That abundance could reduce dependence on lithium mining and price fluctuations. Sodium-ion cells can also use aluminum current collectors on both electrodes, potentially reducing their reliance on copper. Some designs avoid lithium, cobalt, and graphite altogether. More from Energy See All However, sodium-ion batteries are not automatically free of critical minerals. Certain commercial cathode chemistries still use materials such as nickel and manganese, while their hard-carbon anodes require specialized manufacturing. The supply chain for these components is also much less mature. The International Energy Agency (IEA) notes that sodium-ion battery production remains heavily concentrated in China, despite the potential for more geographically diverse raw-material supplies. Lithium-ion still has the energy-density advantage For electric vehicles, one of the most important measures is energy density. It measures how much energy a battery can store relative to its weight or volume. Here, lithium-ion remains ahead. According to the IEA’s 2026 assessment, the latest sodium-ion cells can reach around 175 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg). By comparison, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells can reach approximately 205 Wh/kg, while nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries can reach around 265 Wh/kg. A less energy-dense battery needs to be larger or heavier to store the same amount of energy. In a vehicle, this can mean less driving range or less space for passengers and cargo. The IEA estimates that an average SUV equipped with sodium-ion batteries could achieve up to 350 kilometers (217 miles) of range, compared with approximately 400-600 kilometers (249–373 miles) for lithium-ion vehicles under average weather conditions. Sodium-ion batteries do have an important advantage in colder environments. The latest cells can retain around 90 percent of their nominal capacity at temperatures as low as -40°C (-40°F), outperforming conventional lithium-ion chemistries, particularly LFP. This could make them useful in cold-weather vehicles and equipment. The competition is shifting toward specific applications Sodium-ion’s strongest near-term opportunity may not be replacing the battery in every electric car. Instead, it could find a place in smaller vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, urban delivery fleets, and stationary energy storage, where weight and volume are sometimes less restrictive. The grid-storage market is particularly interesting. Batteries used to store electricity from solar and wind installations do not need to fit inside a vehicle or maximize driving range. Cost, safety, durability, and reliable performance can matter more than energy density. CATL’s 60 GWh agreement with HyperStrong reflects this opportunity, while its TENER sodium-ion storage system, unveiled in June 2026, points to growing interest in commercial-scale stationary applications. Still, the economics are not settled. Lithium-ion manufacturing has benefited from decades of investment and enormous production volumes. In particular, LFP batteries have become highly cost-competitive, making it difficult for sodium-ion to win simply because sodium is cheaper and more abundant. The IEA says global sodium-ion production in 2025 was less than 1 percent of lithium-ion output. Even announced projects for 2030 represent only a fraction of planned lithium-ion manufacturing capacity. A second battery chemistry, not necessarily a replacement The arrival of sodium-ion batteries is important, but it does not mean lithium-ion is about to lose its dominant position. Lithium-based cells continue to improve, while sodium-ion manufacturers still need to scale production, refine materials, and demonstrate consistent performance. The more likely outcome is a battery industry with multiple chemistries serving different needs. Lithium-ion will remain attractive where range, weight and energy density are priorities. Sodium-ion could become increasingly useful where cold-weather performance, material availability and supply-chain diversification carry greater value. Right now, sodium-ion’s biggest achievement may be giving battery manufacturers another option. And in an industry increasingly shaped by the demand for electric vehicles and grid storage, having more than one viable chemistry could prove just as important as developing a better battery.

artigo.texto: Real estate titans are eagerly watching the upcoming Texas gubernatorial race in anticipation of potential changes to the state's policy on data center development. The asset class dominated discussion on the real estate panel at the Bloomberg Invest conference at the Joule Hotel in Downtown Dallas on Tuesday. When the moderator (former TRDer Joe Lovinger) asked if anything could stymie Texas' growth story, Crow Holdings' Michael Hyun pointed to data center regulation: "If there is a significant slowdown in that development, it affects so many areas of the Texas economy." It's something of a double-edged sword for someone like Hyun, who also noted that the frenzy has drawn real estate's finite resources to the buzzy asset class. "You're competing for many of the same contractors to develop your site and guess who can pay more?" he asked. Still, he characterized a crackdown on data center development as "economic suicide." In the lead up to the midterm elections, Gov. Greg Abbott, facing a viable challenger in Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa, veered from his typical pro-business stance and responded to community outrage over data development. He directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt approvals for data center projects and ordered the Public Utility Commission of Texas to audit pending projects. Even so, at least $9 million or 13 percent of the money he's raised since July 2025 came from data center developers or entities tied to data center development, the Texas Tribune reported. Hinojosa has characterized Abbott's actions as temporary moves in service of attracting voters. She says she supports strict legislative guardrails for data center development to protect water supply and grid capacity and curb tax breaks. Laura Hines-Pierce, the co-CEO of Houston-based Hines, was also on the Bloomberg Invest panel. She said the issue isn't as binary as being for or against data centers. According to Hines-Pierce, part of the gray area is in the domain of developer responsibility. "Data centers don't need to be a Star Wars ship that landed in the middle of a community," Hines-Pearce said. DFW tops real estate markets to watch list … again North Texas topped the list of markets to watch for the third consecutive year in a report from the Urban Land Institute and PricewaterhouseCoopers. The report points to robust industrial development — including data centers — as well as corporate relocations and the rise of Y'all Street.

artigo.texto: Everyone treats Contemporary Amperex Technology, better known as CATL, as just a massive electric vehicle battery supplier. That assumption misses the entire trajectory of where the company is actually heading. As EV sales growth normalizes globally, the world's largest battery maker isn't just sitting back to wait for the next automotive boom. They are aggressively restructuring their business model around two pillars: high-capacity energy storage systems (BESS) and standardized battery swapping networks like their Choco-Swap system. If you want to understand how the next wave of the energy transition works, you have to look past standard passenger car cells. CATL is turning batteries from simple automotive components into fluid financial assets and grid-balancing machinery. The Energy Storage Shift Nobody Talks About While media headlines obsess over monthly EV delivery numbers, CATL's utility-scale energy storage business has quietly exploded. Power grids everywhere are straining under the weight of intermittent renewable generation like wind and solar. You cannot run a modern grid on sunshine and good intentions without massive stationary storage backing it up. CATL didn't just stumble into this market. Their TENER energy storage platform, which offers large-scale capacity with zero degradation over the initial years of operation, has completely changed what utility providers expect from hardware. Look at the massive supply deals they've locked inâsuch as multi-gigawatt-hour agreements with global integrators and partners like HyperStrong and international energy giants. The economics here are entirely different from passenger cars. Energy storage buyers care about lifecycle costs, thermal safety, and footprint efficiency. By pushing standardized lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry into massive utility containers and even pivoting automotive manufacturing linesâsuch as adapting facilities originally slated for EV cells toward stationary storage productsâCATL is insulating itself against cyclical slowdowns in consumer car sales. When consumer auto demand dips, grid infrastructure spending picks up the slack. Cracking the Code on Battery Swapping For years, skeptics dismissed battery swapping as an expensive, fragmented niche dominated only by stubborn pioneers like Nio. The hurdles were obvious: every car maker built different vehicle architectures, proprietary pack sizes, and distinct mounting points. Standardization seemed impossible. Then CATL introduced Choco-Swap, introducing standardized 20# and 25# modular battery blocks designed to fit multiple vehicle types. Instead of forcing a single car brand to own the entire ecosystem, CATL acts as an independent banker of energy. Here is why this model actually works in practice: - Fleet operators can swap a depleted pack in minutes, eliminating range anxiety and severe vehicle downtime. - Drivers can subscribe to modular blocks based on their actual mileage needs rather than paying upfront for a massive, expensive solid pack they rarely fully utilize. - The physical battery blocks inside the swap stations double as decentralized energy storage units, feeding power back into the grid during peak demand hours. Building thousands of swap stations requires serious capital. But CATL isn't treating these stations as mere fueling stops. They are physical nodes in a distributed virtual power plant. The Financialization of Energy What makes CATL genuinely formidable is how they manage risk. Through their battery asset management framework, they track real-time health data across millions of active cells using cloud diagnostics. This data allows them to evaluate credit, price flexible subscription plans, and offer precise buy-back guarantees based on residual battery health. When a battery is no longer fit for high-performance passenger vehicle driving, it gets pulled from the rotation and redeployed into a stationary energy storage container for grid backup. Finally, it heads to recycling facilities to recover critical lithium, cobalt, and nickel. It's a closed-loop financial and physical ecosystem. Competitors who only sell raw hardware are fighting a margin race to the bottom. CATL is building a recurring revenue model that stretches across the entire lifecycle of a mineral. Geopolitical Realities and Supply Chain Control You cannot talk about CATL without addressing the heavy friction of global trade politics. Western markets are throwing up tariffs, domestic content requirements, and strict regulatory walls to keep Chinese clean-tech dominance at bay. Yet, CATL keeps finding operational workarounds. Instead of direct exports, they rely on technology licensing agreements, localized joint ventures, and massive vertical integration projectsâsuch as their multi-billion-dollar investments in raw material extraction and processing hubs in Indonesia. By locking down the supply chain from nickel mining all the way to grid-scale software management, they maintain cost advantages that Western manufacturers struggle to match. The strategy is pragmatic. If you cannot easily export finished packs into a specific market due to trade rules, you license the tech, supply the core components, or pivot local production lines toward stationary storage, which often faces different regulatory classifications than passenger automotive batteries. What Comes Next CATL's next phase of growth won't be defined by how many passenger cars roll off assembly lines with their logos on the pack. It will be determined by how deeply they embed themselves into the fabric of global energy infrastructure. By scaling modular battery swapping for urban mobility and blanketing utility grids with high-performance storage blocks, they are transforming from a simple manufacturer into an essential energy utility. If you're betting against them because car sales wobble for a few quarters, you're missing the entire board.

artigo.texto: Massive AI Data Center Sparks Backlash Despite Clean Energy Promises As more governments put increasing pressure on tech companies to develop more sustainable data centres, to ensure they do not place a further burden on the grid, several tech firms are investing in developing new energy capacity and incorporating other innovative ideas into their facility development. This has led Google to suggest that the development of its new U.S. data centre in Minnesota, and associated energy development, will have a positive benefit on the region's transmission network. Google has proposed an agreement with Xcel Energy to support significant wind, solar and battery storage development alongside its new 780-MW Project Skyway data centre. The tech giant plans to finance Xcel's addition of 1.4 GW of wind, 200 MW of solar power and 300 MW of battery storage to the grid. While the combined capacity of these projects exceeds the data centre's projected electricity demand, wind and solar generation fluctuate depending on weather conditions, and battery storage does not generate additional electricity. Xcel Energy says the new energy resources will serve the wider grid, benefiting other customers as well as the data centre. Google plans to cover the associated costs under the proposed agreement, including payments for capacity it does not fully use. The aim is to get the residents of Pine Island, Minnesota, on board with its development plans, particularly as 71 per cent of Americans surveyed in a Gallup poll earlier this year opposed the construction of a data centre in their local area. Developing such a significant renewable energy project will also help Google meet its target of operating entirely on carbon-free energy by 2030. The proposed agreement includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, meaning that Google will be required to finance the development of the infrastructure even if the demand for AI decreases. Under the proposed agreement, Google would pay minimum monthly charges based on at least 75 per cent of its contracted capacity, even if its electricity consumption falls below that level. If the company terminates the agreement early, it could face exit fees equivalent to as much as eight years of minimum demand charges. Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy, explained, "Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power… That's where these protections come in." The Clean Energy Accelerator Charge (CEAC) agreement model uses the same structure as the Clean Transition Tariff (CTT) Google developed with NV Energy. It is currently pending approval from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission. In its statement about the agreement, Google's Head of Energy Market Innovation, Briana Kobor, said, "Google's partnership with Xcel Energy reimagines how data centres can be served, enabling us to be a catalyst for electricity innovation and helping to ensure our growth supports a cleaner, more affordable energy future for the communities we call home." The rapid rollout of data centres in the United States is driving up the country's electricity demand to unprecedented levels. The U.S. DOE Office of Science national laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, estimates that data centres could account for 11.8 per cent of total U.S. electricity by 2030. Meanwhile, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects that electricity consumed by data centre servers could reach between 446 billion and 818 billion kilowatt-hours (BkWh) annually by 2050, accounting for between 22 per cent and 33 per cent of commercial building electricity consumption. This is driving demand for new clean energy capacity to ensure that data centres are not powered by fossil fuels – although several companies still depend on gas-powered plants. As utilities respond to the growing power demand by rapidly building out the grid, which costs billions of dollars to do, they are ultimately expecting the demand for AI data centres to continue. However, if the demand for AI wanes or the government decides to regulate the sector more strictly, electricity demand could fall, potentially leaving consumers to foot the bill for infrastructure upgrades. In addition, the use of clean power in data centre operations is not the only sustainability concern. In October last year, the Minnesota Centre for Environmental Advocacy filed a lawsuit against the city of Pine Island, claiming that the environmental study for the development was vague, initially omitted Google as the end user, and failed to disclose impacts on energy, water, noise, and generators. The initial Alternative Urban Area Review (AUAR) indicated that the new data centre would use approximately 55.7 million gallons of water per year, thereby increasing the city's total water consumption by approximately 50 per cent. Meanwhile, environmental groups have voiced concerns about the lack of comprehensive groundwater impact analysis. Meanwhile, opponents have questioned whether wastewater discharges may potentially run into the Zumbro River. In a Pine Island survey conducted between 1st and 31st August, 75.8 per cent of participants are against the construction of Project Skyway. While Google has made bold promises to upgrade the grid through clean energy projects, residents and environmental groups have broader concerns about consumer protections and the projects' environmental impact. So, while Google may be attempting to develop a more "sustainable" data centre, it is failing to win over local residents, who remain concerned about the long-term implications of building a giant AI data centre. artigo.texto: TerraVolt Holdings, Inc., an infrastructure developer specializing in powered land solutions for data centers, has executed option agreements to purchase 1,077 acres of land outside the town of Declo in Cassia County, Idaho, on which it intends to develop a behind-the-meter digital infrastructure campus. The company said in a press release that the property was zoned for multiple use and was situated near long-haul fiber routes and the Williams Northwest Pipeline. The campus will have an initial 240 MW of dedicated on-site power generation, backed by TerraVolt’s previously announced firm natural gas supply agreement of 55,000 MMBtu per day. “These option agreements secure site control, allowing our team to advance land use plans, environmental due diligence, power plant, electrical distribution, and water treatment system designs, and county and state permitting,” said Joel Stone, TerraVolt Holding Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. “By pairing a strategic, expansive land parcel directly with firm gas supply and pipeline access, we are addressing the single largest bottleneck in the digital economy: the multi-year wait for large-load grid interconnections.” With on-site, islanded power generation, the proposed campus will avoid utility interconnection delays. In states like Texas, data center developments that require grid interconnection face lengthy delays, with w.media reporting in September that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas was tracking 438 GW of large load requests, 89 percent of which were for data centers. TerraVolt said the behind-the-meter deployment will reduce the time-to-power schedule for hyperscale and neocloud deployments and protect existing ratepayers from grid strain or rate increases. TerraVolt plans to sell shovel-ready building sites to data center operators, providing power, fiber, potable and fire-protection water, wastewater treatment, and other site services under long-term infrastructure services agreements.TerraVolt also intends to require low water usage for any data center developments on the property, making it a condition of sale for each site. “We look forward to working closely with Cassia County officials and the local community to deliver responsible, long-term industrial tax base growth without impacting local power rates or the agricultural water the region depends on. That is why every building on this campus will be required to use cooling technologies with low water usage,” said Stone. According to Data Center Map, there are currently 25 data centers under development or operational in Idaho. The state is also home to Meta’s Kuna Data Center, a more than US$ 1.2 billion investment, which became operational on September 3, 2026.

artigo.texto: Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76. When New York became the first state in the country to enact a moratorium on data center development, Adrienne Yocina was excited. For the past two years, the mom of three has been organizing in western Genesee County to stop a 600-megawatt data center from coming to a site close to the Tonawanda Seneca Nation’s reservation and a federal wildlife refuge. But almost four months after the one-year moratorium began, Yocina tells me that she’s “getting nervous.” She’s worried that Democratic governor Kathy Hochul won’t sign a stronger bill to impose a stricter moratorium, and is concerned that the state Department of Environmental Conservation is not adequately involved in the process of evaluating data centers in New York. “I feel like she’s just trying to shut us up,” she says of Hochul. Data centers are at the center of midterm races across the country, with politicians of both parties making promises to enact regulations or moratoriums on development. After next week comes the tough part: Newly elected officials must either break their word or follow through on those promises as they weigh large infrastructure projects coming to their states and residents who say they’ll reject data centers no matter what. How will those compromises go—and will they appease voters? New York’s moratorium, and the continued opposition from some groups, may offer clues. In July, just two months after dismissing the idea of a data center moratorium, Hochul signed the nation’s first executive order to put a pause on development. Her order was a compromise. Just weeks prior, the state legislature had passed an omnibus bill that would have implemented a one-year moratorium throughout New York. The bill contained several provisions that made it more aggressive than Hochul’s moratorium, including stricter limits on the size of data centers and a mandate that the Department of Environmental Conservation conduct a thorough environmental impact review of data center operations. Rather than sign the bill, Hochul issued her own order. (The governor has until the end of the year to sign that bill, and her office says they are still looking at it.) One of the bill’s State Senate sponsors, Democrat Kristen Gonzalez, has been publicly supportive of Hochul’s moratorium. The governor’s office, Gonzalez says, proactively reached out to her after her bill passed to help design the moratorium for more immediate relief for New Yorkers. Gonzalez went on a data center tour of New York at the end of the summer, talking to residents around the state about their concerns. She told me that the people she talked to overwhelmingly wanted Hochul to go further and implement more aggressive measures to protect communities from data centers. “There are local communities statewide that are living near existing data centers, dealing with significant air pollution and noise pollution, who are struggling with rising utility bills and rising water bills,” she told me. “We see the moratorium as a first step, but it can’t be the last.” Hochul has a comfortable lead over Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman ahead of Tuesday’s election—something that may have been helped by the moratorium’s passing. In a recent Quinnipiac poll of New York voters, 53 percent of respondents said they trusted Hochul to do a better job in handling AI and data centers, compared to just 31 percent trusting Blakeman. Blakeman, who has voiced support for data centers, called Hochul’s moratorium “crazy” when it was passed in July. His campaign didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. Hochul has also touted her tough-on-data-center bona fides on the campaign trail. Early last month, she hosted a roundtable discussion on data centers with agricultural, environmental, and business leaders at a farm in the Hudson Valley. There, she told reporters that she wanted to work with the state legislature to implement more aggressive protections, including banning tax breaks for data centers. At the event, Hochul was flanked by Gonzalez and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of Washington’s most prominent data center critics. I asked Hochul at the event how she anticipates handling continued opposition after her moratorium ends. How does New York balance economic development with community opposition if some people don’t want data centers in their backyards under any circumstances, even with the assurances from the state that Hochul’s office is working to create? The purpose of her pause, she said, was that communities should be able to choose. “This is democracy in action,” she said. “If you want it, it should come with all kinds of guardrails and restraints, but if you don’t want it, it doesn’t come.” More New Yorkers may end up choosing the latter option. A Siena poll from September found that 63 percent of New Yorkers would oppose data centers being built in their area even after Hochul’s moratorium expires. (It’s even higher for New York Democrats, with 75 percent saying they’d remain opposed to data center development post-moratorium.) Many newly elected (or reelected) governors will face a similar dynamic: At least 20 gubernatorial candidates have promised a data center moratorium or pause, according to research compiled by government relations company MultiState. Even more have promised to regulate the industry more tightly. Formerly data-center-friendly incumbents like Texas’s Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro have also made pledges to be stricter on their development. artigo.texto: On October 27, 2026, CATL reportedly told investors that its all-solid-state battery development had moved from a 10 Ah-class validation platform to trials of 20 Ah samples. CarNewsChina attributed the cell-stage detail to Y-Auto. The reported step marks progress in development, while CATL’s next production milestones remain future targets. What the 20 Ah samples mean Amp-hours (Ah) measure a cell’s electric-charge capacity. The reported move from a 10 Ah-class validation platform to 20 Ah sample trials describes a change in the cells under development, not a vehicle performance result. Production targets, not a vehicle launch date Reports put CATL’s target for small-batch production in 2027 and its plan for large-scale manufacturing around 2030. These are manufacturing milestones; they do not give a date for a consumer vehicle using the cells. The program is also reported to target an energy density of about 500 Wh/kg. Energy density measures energy relative to mass. That cell-level target is distinct from a vehicle’s driving range, which is a vehicle-level result. Engineering hurdles in solid-state cells For solid-state batteries that use sulfide materials, maintaining contact between solid components is one engineering challenge. Electrodes expand and contract during charging and discharging, which can disrupt that contact. Sulfide materials also require moisture control because reactions involving them can release toxic hydrogen sulfide. Durability, manufacturing yield, cost, safety and real-world performance are further development considerations.

artigo.texto: AI Models & Platforms Envision Deploys SST-Based 800V DC Power at Ulanqab AI Data Center Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google Envision said on Nov. 2, 2026, that an integrated 800-volt direct-current (800V DC) power system is now powering live computing workloads at its Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, China, a deployment the company described in its announcement as the world’s first commercial use of such a system in a large-scale AI data center. The announcement says the system delivers power end to end, from medium-voltage AC input to the server rack, and that it is already operating commercially ahead of wider industry adoption, providing a reference for AI data centers moving to 800V DC power infrastructure. Solid-State Transformers and Real-Time Coordination The newly deployed system integrates three hardware layers: solid-state transformers (SST), battery energy storage (BESS), and equipment that adjusts direct-current voltage for computing hardware. Coordinating them is Envision’s Dubhe Controller, which runs with the company’s Dubhe Energy Foundation Model and adjusts the transformers and batteries in real time so that power supply tracks computing demand, including abrupt swings in load. According to Envision, the deployment is built around three capabilities: stable SST conversion directly from 10-kilovolt medium voltage to an 800V DC bus across operating conditions; battery storage that provides both second-scale power support and minute-scale backup; and millisecond-level coordination between SST and storage that absorbs GPU load fluctuations locally. Envision said the 800V DC architecture simplifies AI data center power systems, citing higher power conversion and watt-to-bit efficiency, a more compact equipment footprint, and reduced cabling and copper requirements. Those advantages, the company said, can lower infrastructure costs and support higher computing density within the same space. Rising Power Demand Per Rack The announcement frames the deployment against a specific operational problem: as AI computing demand accelerates, operators must deliver more power to each rack within constrained space while keeping supply stable as computing loads swing sharply from moment to moment. “AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage, and the grid to meet computing demand,” said Kevin Huang, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of Energy Storage and AIDC Power Systems. Huang said the live system demonstrates an end-to-end architecture connecting renewable supply with computing demand, calling it a critical step in moving power-compute coordination from strategic vision to day-to-day operating practice. Galaxy Campus and Mission Gobi The Galaxy campus, in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, began operations in August 2026, when Envision commissioned the site on Aug. 6 anchored by a 120,000-square-meter AI supercomputing facility, according to the company’s commissioning announcement at the time. That record described the campus as designed to scale to over 2GW of capacity; the Nov. 2 release states a planned capacity of 3GW and says the campus is designed to support up to one million AI accelerators operating in parallel at full build-out, with more than 80% of its power planned to come from direct renewable electricity connections. Envision’s Galaxy campus page markets the site as a net-zero AI data center, advertising long-term fixed electricity pricing at 20% below grid rates under a 10-year price lock, bundled electricity and green certificates, and a 60% green power direct-supply ratio. Envision said it aims to scale the approach through Mission Gobi, an initiative unveiled at VivaTech in Paris in June 2026 with Galaxy as its first flagship project. Mission Gobi targets 5GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030, and the company presents it as a replicable blueprint, arguing that developing even 1% of global desert and Gobi regions could support computing capacity at terawatt scale at highly competitive cost.

artigo.texto: Why Battery Storage Developers Target Retiring Baseload Sites Some storage developers are acquiring retired coal and nuclear power stations to reuse the grid connections they already hold. Before any batteries arrive, the buyer faces a demanding first task — dismantling and remediating a station built for another era. The Interconnection Queue and the Appeal of Retired Plants In its 2026 Queued Up analysis, Berkeley Lab found median timelines above five years from interconnection request to commercial operation for projects built in 2025 in regions with available data. Only 13% of the capacity requesting interconnection between 2000 and 2020 reached commercial operation. By contrast, 75% was withdrawn, and 10% remains active. At the end of 2025, queues held roughly 1,312 GW of generation and 749 GW of storage. A retiring plant can offer a route around the queue. Retired baseload sites are especially valuable because their transmission infrastructure was built to move large, steady power output from centralized plants. For storage and renewable developers, that legacy capacity can reduce the need to build new high-voltage connections from scratch and make the site easier to evaluate for future grid use. At regulated facilities, ash management units are subject to groundwater monitoring and corrective action obligations, with closure and post-closure care to follow. Because the interconnection point and substation already exist, a buyer can pursue the reuse of those assets. In New York, Bear Peak Power’s proposed 200-MW, four-hour system at the former Cayuga coal plant would reuse the existing interconnection and substation on a 5.7-acre site. At Mt. Tom in Holyoke, Massachusetts, a 3 MW, 6 MWh lithium-ion system has operated since 2018 on a site where the coal plant closed in 2014. In Hawaii, Plus Power’s 185 MW, 565 MWh system in Kapolei sits on about eight acres at the site of an AES coal plant closed in 2022. In New Jersey, Starwood Energy plans to use the Logan plant’s interconnection rights to connect new offshore wind transmission lines, extending the logic beyond storage. Retired and retiring plants often serve as points of interconnection to the electricity grid, along with transportation access, according to a 2025 Department of Energy post. The same post cites a 44 MW solar project at a retired coal site in Coffeen, Illinois. Aging transmission assets are driving demand for grid upgrades across the network. A site with an existing connection can offer a path to add capacity as upgrade work proceeds. Repurposing Retired Fossil Fuel Plants Means Managing Coal Ash At coal sites, ash adds a regulatory obligation. A 2024 final rule covers legacy coal ash impoundments at inactive electric utilities. Under the rule, owners must meet the requirements that apply to inactive impoundments at active facilities, except for location restrictions and liner design criteria. At regulated facilities, ash management units are subject to groundwater monitoring and corrective action obligations, with closure and post-closure care to follow. Legacy units are more likely to be unlined and unmonitored than those at operating plants, according to the agency. Since the rule, timelines have shifted. A February 2026 extension pushed groundwater monitoring system installation at ash management units to February 2031 and the start of closure to February 2032. A further amendment proposal followed in April 2026. Limited monitoring at legacy units leaves buyers with unknowns. Baseline groundwater sampling before closing can inform the purchase price. Closure design and storage layout should be developed together. Careful demolition planning should preserve the switchyard and high-voltage tie lines. Their loss would forfeit the premise of the acquisition. Converting Decommissioned Nuclear to Battery Storage Follows the NRC’s Clock Under NRC rules, decommissioning must finish within 60 years of shutdown. Owners are free to combine immediate and deferred dismantling. A license termination plan, due within two years of the expected license termination, documents the remaining dismantlement and final radiation surveys. Final approval requires a license amendment, an opportunity for a hearing, and a public meeting near the plant. Most plans target unrestricted use, meaning a residual radiation dose below 25 millirems per year. Where criteria are met, licensees may sell land and keep a small parcel under license for spent fuel storage. Such installations remain under NRC regulation, with licensees responsible for security and funding. Each licensee also reports decommissioning funding status to the agency every two years. In deferred monitoring, a site may stay restricted for an extended period. Early negotiation over access to non-radiological parcels can be a practical path. Safe Dismantling Depends on Continuous Ventilation Throughout dismantling, crews must keep ventilation systems running because radioactivity stays sealed in through their continued operation. Before work begins, authorities review safety concepts for handling and transport. Continuous ventilation demands reliable power. To avoid gaps, developers should confirm with the owner how the site’s electrical service will be maintained. A negotiated early transfer of the switchyard parcel could allow battery construction to begin as the remaining dismantling continues. At the former Vermont Yankee site in Vernon, PowerTransitions is pursuing a large battery energy storage system on about 140 acres along the Connecticut River. Spent fuel sits in 58 dry storage casks on-site until the federal government selects a permanent repository. Any battery layout will need to account for the licensed parcel and its security boundary. Since acquiring the closed plant in 2019, NorthStar Group Services has owned the property. The developer holds an agreement to potentially lease it.
