artigo.texto: The Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (GERC) has adopted the tariffs discovered through a competitive bidding process for the development of a 450 MW / 900 MWh standalone Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Gujarat. The approval covers projects allocated to NLC India Renewables Limited and Sun Drops Energia Limited under Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited’s (GUVNL) Phase-IX battery storage procurement initiative. The petition was filed by GUVNL before the Commission under Sections 63 and 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act, 2003, seeking approval for the discovered tariffs. The procurement process was initiated after a developer selected under the earlier Phase-VII tender failed to execute the required Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA) for the 900 MWh capacity. Following approval from the Ministry of Power, Government of India, GUVNL issued a fresh Request for Selection (RfS) on June 22, 2026, under Phase-IX. The projects are supported through Viability Gap Funding (VGF) provided under the Power System Development Fund (PSDF), aimed at encouraging the deployment of battery storage infrastructure. The tender received 11 online bids, of which 10 bidders successfully met the technical and financial qualification requirements. Subsequently, an e-reverse auction was conducted on August 11, 2026, with nine eligible bidders participating in the competitive bidding process. The successful capacities were allocated through a bucket-filling approach based on the L1 discovered tariff, with a two percent margin. Under the final allocation, NLC India Renewables Limited has been awarded 275 MW / 550 MWh of battery storage capacity at a discovered monthly storage rate of ₹231,989 per MW. Sun Drops Energia Limited has secured the remaining 175 MW / 350 MWh capacity at a monthly storage rate of ₹231,990 per MW. Both successful bidders submitted affidavits before the Commission confirming that they had no objections to the adoption of the discovered tariffs. After examining the bidding process and submissions made by the parties, GERC approved the tariffs for both developers under the provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003. GUVNL highlighted that the proposed battery storage projects will support Gujarat in meeting its Energy Storage Obligations (ESO) and Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPO). The installations are also expected to strengthen grid stability, improve power balancing and address the variability associated with renewable energy generation. As part of its directions, GERC has instructed GUVNL to execute the BESPAs with the successful developers within the stipulated timeframe. The agreements must incorporate appropriate provisions under the Electricity (Late Payment Surcharge) Rules. GUVNL has also been directed to submit copies of the executed agreements to the Commission and publish the final tariff structures on its official website to ensure transparency. With the tariff adoption approved, GERC has disposed of the petition, clearing the way for the implementation of the 450 MW / 900 MWh standalone battery storage projects in Gujarat. artigo.texto: Some residents of a proposed large data center in Enid are planning a petition drive for a recall of the City Council and Mayor who supported a data center project proposed by some local business officials while Yukon voters will decide this week on the fate of their mayor in a similar protest. While the Project Thunderbird data center proposed by Jason Singer, Aaron Singer, Chad Dillingham and Troy Phillips who make up the firm Plainsmen Holdings, has the support of the Enid Regional Development Alliance, it doesn’t have the support of some residents. The group, No Data Centers in Enid, is led by Jacob McNew, who recently said the organization has launched efforts to recall Mayor David Mason and most city commissioners. A petition effort was held Sunday in Enid to force a vote of residents to overturn the rezoning of two properties where the data center project would be located. We are seeking committed volunteers who can get involved in this campaign. As we enter a new phase of this fight, we are needing folks who can help out. There are tons of ways to get involved. Many of which don’t require a lot of time. If you or anyone you know would like to get experience in activism, please reach out! This is a great opportunity for young and old to make a difference in our community,” shared the group in a social media posting over the weekend. It followed an earlier posting. “We would like to take the time to address the biggest piece of misinformation that we frequently see online and hear in person. It is imperative that we oppose this project using only facts. Project Thunderbird is not a “done deal”. While Mayor David Mason, City Manager Jerald Gilbert and City Attorney Melissa Blanton have been in contact with Plainsmen Holdings LLC since at least January 2026, as their NDAs prove, they do not have the power alone to accept this proposal. Although they have made it quite apparent, they are not impartial to this project, it still requires city commissioners to decide whether it gets approval or not. There are more opportunities to fight back on the proposal, and we will share those opportunities on this page as they are announced. As of now, we are collecting signatures for recalls as well as a referendum to overturn the city council vote that approved the rezonings.” No Data Centers in Enid originally announced its opposition saying it wants to keep health and quality of life and that no possible tax income was worth the sacrifice. “People want to stay living in their homes, farming on their farms to provide healthy food for our people and running the ranches that provide food. We want to continue to know our kids are healthy and able to focus at school. We want to keep looking up at night to enjoy our beautiful clear and clean pollution free sky!” Project Thunderbird would sit on a 1,735 acre site and the developers say it would use behind-the-meter electricity generation. In their original announcement in September, they said the project would rely on raw pipeline water from Kaw Lake located 8 miles east of Ponca City. A similar recall election petition was successful in the city of Yukon over a proposed Beltline Energy data center that drew large opposition. City voters will decide Tuesday, November 3 on a recall of Mayor Brian Pilmore. Residents launched their recall petition in May. In addition, a petition to require voter approval for the proposed data center was recently filed with the Yukon City Clerk, according to the Yukon Progress. “It’s the most democratic way to deal with these things,” explained petition proponent Charles Scott. He said the vote would not be for a prohibition but for approval. Scott also said the petition contained 354 signatures while only 162 were required. City officials were reported to be in the process of verifying the validity of the signatures. The recall drive in Yukon already resulted in the resignation of Vice Mayor Jeff Wooton shortly after the recall effort targeted him and Mayor Pilmore. He resigned June 6, 2026.

The global salt hydrates market is entering a phase of sustained expansion as demand for efficient thermal management and energy storage accelerates across buildings, industry, and renewable energy integration. Salt hydrates, including sodium sulfate decahydrate, calcium chloride hexahydrate, magnesium sulfate heptahydrate, and sodium acetate trihydrate, are increasingly valued for their ability to store and release latent heat at precise temperature ranges, making them central to phase change material (PCM) solutions. As of 2025, the market is supported by decarbonization policies, rising electricity costs, and the need to balance intermittent renewable supply with demand. The forecast period 2026–2035 points to continued growth, with thermal energy storage in construction and industrial processes acting as the primary demand engine. However, the market faces headwinds from alternative PCM materials, raw material price volatility, and technical challenges such as phase segregation and supercooling. This report provides a data-driven view of market size, structure, end-use dynamics, and regional trends, offering stakeholders a transparent framework to navigate the evolving salt hydrates landscape. The baseline scenario for the world salt hydrates market anticipates steady growth from 2026 to 2035, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 5.8% and a market index reaching 176 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is anchored in the accelerating deployment of thermal energy storage (TES) systems, particularly in the construction sector where salt hydrate-based PCMs are integrated into building envelopes, underfloor heating, and cooling systems to shift peak loads and improve energy efficiency. Industrial applications, including chemical synthesis and dehydrating agents, provide a stable demand base, while pharmaceutical excipients and food additives contribute niche but consistent volume. In 2025, demand is concentrated in building applications such as PCM-enhanced wallboards, underfloor heating, and cold storage, where salt hydrates absorb and release latent heat to shift peak loads and improve energy efficiency. The mechanism is straightforward: during off-peak hours or when renewable generation is abundant, the hydrate melts, storing thermal energy; during peak demand, it solidifies, releasing heat. This capability is increasingly valued as electricity grids face stress from intermittent renewables and rising cooling demand. artigo.texto: An out-of-town data center development firm has locked down a 180-acre site approved last year for a data center campus on the Powhatan-Chesterfield line. An entity tied to Vantage Data Centers out of Colorado last month paid roughly $9.4 million for an assemblage that’s planned to eventually house the Powhatan Technology Park. The property, the majority of which is located at 1318 Page Road, was approved two years ago for a 120-acre data center project that was proposed by California-based Province Group. Then, in October of 2025, Province Group received approvals to tack on 60 additional acres to the original project site for an overall 180-acre campus. The fully assembled site is on the east side of Page Road, just north of the intersection with Anderson Highway, abutting Chesterfield County. As detailed last year in county staff reports, the total roughly 180 acres were slated to eventually house up to four detached data center buildings with a total of 2 million square feet, in what has been described as the biggest data center project the county has ever had on the table. Per a Powhatan County representative, the sale of the original 120-acre tract closed Oct. 21 for $5.7 million. A sale of the additional roughly 60-acre parcel closed on the same day for $3.65 million. The buyer was Powhatan Technology Park LLC. Vantage Data Centers confirmed its purchase of the Powhatan Tech Park site in an email on Friday. “We are evaluating opportunities for future development at the location, but we do not have any additional details to share at this time,” a company representative wrote to BizSense. “We look forward to engaging with local stakeholders and the community as planning progresses and will share more information when available.” The sale had not yet been reflected in online property records as of Friday afternoon. The previous owner of the 120-acre tract is listed in online property records as New County Line Farm LLC, an entity tied to Harold and Christina Ellis, while the previous owner of the 60-acre parcel is listed as JMS Investments LLC, which is tied to Mark and Deborah Sowers. The nature of the relationship between Province Group and Vantage Data Centers regarding the Powhatan project is unclear; however, in an email late Friday afternoon, a Powhatan County representative confirmed Province Group remains involved in the project. The Powhatan County representative also stated that the county has not yet received a site plan for the project. Province Group CEO Mark Kerslake presented the application for the 60-acre addition to the Powhatan Planning Commission a year ago. In his presentation, he noted that Province Group had an end user lined up for the previously rezoned 120-acre parcel, though it was not clear who that end user was. As of last year, buildout of the overall project from Province Group was anticipated to occur in multiple phases and take at least five years to complete. Vantage was founded in 2010, and has developed dozens of data center campuses across the U.S. and around the world. According to company’s website, it has developed or is developing three data centers in Ashburn in Northern Virginia and one in Fredericksburg. Province Group was founded in 1991 and is headquartered in Newport Beach, California. The website states that it has developed, renovated, acquired or entitled more than 75 projects with a combined value of more than $850 million, including projects in states like California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia and Washington. The proposed Powhatan project was seemingly the company’s first development in the Richmond area. Elsewhere in the region, data center news abounds. Google revealed publicly last week that it is currently doing due diligence on a roughly 1,000-acre site within West Creek Business Park in Goochland County for a potential, 1,200-megawatt data center development. The announcement comes as several other data center developments within Goochland’s tech overlay district are being weighed, to the concern of hundreds of residents on both sides of the Goochland-Henrico county line. Google has also begun construction on a data center campus on a 300-plus-acre site at 2700 Bermuda Hundred Road in eastern Chesterfield next to Meadowville Technology Park, and has several other data center facilities planned for the western end of Chesterfield.

artigo.texto: 7x24 Fall 2026: AI Frontier Futurist Meets Data Center OG Key Highlights - Nabeel Mahmood framed the Fifth Compute as a transition from conventional computing toward autonomous intelligence, while warning that technological capabilities are advancing faster than the physical infrastructure supporting them. - Mahmood identified power, cooling, connectivity, autonomous-system reliability, and human capital as interconnected constraints, while calling for greater transparency, community trust, and engineering discipline. - James Coe and a team from Legacy Investing and Gardner Builders demonstrated how a 1988 Minneapolis data center was converted for 20 MW of AI workloads, with the first 5 MW ready for service in just four months. - The Minneapolis conversion employed procurement-driven engineering, unconventional equipment integration, and phased construction to accelerate deployment while maintaining operations for existing tenants. - Both presentations underscored the continuing importance of mission-critical reliability and experienced engineering judgment as the industry moves into increasingly complex AI infrastructure environments. SAN ANTONIO, Texas — On Tuesday morning at the 7x24 Exchange Fall 2026 Conference, Nabeel Mahmood invited the data center industry to imagine a future in which artificial intelligence becomes increasingly autonomous, quantum and biological computing expand the boundaries of technology, and digital infrastructure eventually extends beyond Earth. Ninety minutes after Mahmood's keynote concluded, veteran data center engineer James Coe and his colleagues were explaining how they had removed part of the fifth-floor curtain wall of a nearly 40-year-old Minneapolis building to install massive chillers, while navigating a sprawling electrical and mechanical retrofit that would support 20 megawatts of AI computing capacity. One presentation contemplated humanity's next technological frontier. The other examined what it takes to advance that frontier inside a building constructed before the commercial internet, using equipment and engineering practices accumulated across several generations of computing. The juxtaposition neatly captured the official theme of the 7x24 Exchange conference, The Intersection of Traditional and AI Data Centers. It also illuminated an increasingly consequential reality for digital infrastructure: The pace of computing innovation may be accelerating, but the facilities supporting it must still contend with power availability, thermal performance, construction schedules, equipment compatibility, and the unforgiving requirements of operational reliability. As DCF detailed in its opening-day reporting from 7x24 Exchange Fall 2026, the convergence of agentic AI, increasingly volatile electrical loads, grid reliability concerns, and community opposition was already challenging traditional assumptions about data center infrastructure. The two presentations, however, were less a clash between futurism and traditional engineering than complementary explorations of the same challenge. Mahmood, CEO and managing director of Nomad Futurist, argued that the next era of computing will depend on overcoming constraints embedded in the physical systems and institutions supporting it. Coe, a senior principal at Syska Hennessy Group with decades of data center engineering experience, joined representatives of Legacy Investing and Gardner Builders to demonstrate how those constraints could be addressed through engineering adaptability and the creative reuse of existing infrastructure. The overriding question was not simply how far artificial intelligence might advance, but whether the data center industry can deliver the dependable infrastructure required to sustain that advance. As Mahmood observed during his keynote, "Ambition without execution is simply a presentation." The Fifth Compute: From Information Processing to Autonomous Intelligence In his keynote, The Fifth Compute – Humanity's Next Frontier, Mahmood placed the current AI revolution within a much longer history of technological transformation. Fire expanded humanity's command over energy; steam mechanized labor; electricity enabled modern industrial civilization; and digital computing transformed the processing, storage, and exchange of information. What he calls the Fifth Compute represents another turning point, in which technology increasingly extends human cognitive capabilities rather than simply augmenting physical effort. The significance of this shift, Mahmood suggested, extends well beyond the current enthusiasm for generative AI and the extraordinary investments flowing into accelerated computing infrastructure. He described an emerging convergence of large-scale digital infrastructure, adaptive AI models, autonomous systems, and potentially new computational substrates, including quantum and biological computing. In this environment, machines increasingly become active participants in processes rather than passive tools responding to human instructions. That distinction becomes especially important when intelligence evolves into agency. An AI model may analyze information and recommend a course of action, Mahmood explained, but an autonomous agent can observe conditions, make decisions, execute actions, and learn from their outcomes. Each additional degree of autonomy raises questions about authority, accountability, and the circumstances under which a machine should be permitted to act without human intervention. For data centers, those questions have immediate operational implications. Mahmood offered a hypothetical example in which an intelligent system detects an emerging thermal problem and automatically adjusts cooling distribution, while other systems independently redistribute workloads or modify power allocation. artigo.texto: As more governments put increasing pressure on tech companies to develop more sustainable data centres, to ensure they do not place a further burden on the grid, several tech firms are investing in developing new energy capacity and incorporating other innovative ideas into their facility development. This has led Google to suggest that the development of its new U.S. data centre in Minnesota, and associated energy development, will have a positive benefit on the region’s transmission network. Google has proposed an agreement with Xcel Energy to support significant wind, solar and battery storage development alongside its new 780-MW Project Skyway data centre. The tech giant plans to finance Xcel's addition of 1.4 GW of wind, 200 MW of solar power and 300 MW of battery storage to the grid. While the combined capacity of these projects exceeds the data centre's projected electricity demand, wind and solar generation fluctuate depending on weather conditions, and battery storage does not generate additional electricity. Xcel Energy says the new energy resources will serve the wider grid, benefiting other customers as well as the data centre. Google plans to cover the associated costs under the proposed agreement, including payments for capacity it does not fully use. The aim is to get the residents of Pine Island, Minnesota, on board with its development plans, particularly as 71 per cent of Americans surveyed in a Gallup poll earlier this year opposed the construction of a data centre in their local area. Developing such a significant renewable energy project will also help Google meet its target of operating entirely on carbon-free energy by 2030. The proposed agreement includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, meaning that Google will be required to finance the development of the infrastructure even if the demand for AI decreases. Under the proposed agreement, Google would pay minimum monthly charges based on at least 75 per cent of its contracted capacity, even if its electricity consumption falls below that level. If the company terminates the agreement early, it could face exit fees equivalent to as much as eight years of minimum demand charges. Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy, explained, “Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power… That’s where these protections come in.” The Clean Energy Accelerator Charge (CEAC) agreement model uses the same structure as the Clean Transition Tariff (CTT) Google developed with NV Energy. It is currently pending approval from the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission. In its statement about the agreement, Google’s Head of Energy Market Innovation, Briana Kobor, said, “Google’s partnership with Xcel Energy reimagines how data centres can be served, enabling us to be a catalyst for electricity innovation and helping to ensure our growth supports a cleaner, more affordable energy future for the communities we call home.” The rapid rollout of data centres in the United States is driving up the country’s electricity demand to unprecedented levels. The U.S. DOE Office of Science national laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, estimates that data centres could account for 11.8 per cent of total U.S. electricity by 2030. Meanwhile, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects that electricity consumed by data centre servers could reach between 446 billion and 818 billion kilowatt-hours (BkWh) annually by 2050, accounting for between 22 per cent and 33 per cent of commercial building electricity consumption. This is driving demand for new clean energy capacity to ensure that data centres are not powered by fossil fuels – although several companies still depend on gas-powered plants. As utilities respond to the growing power demand by rapidly building out the grid, which costs billions of dollars to do, they are ultimately expecting the demand for AI data centres to continue. However, if the demand for AI wanes or the government decides to regulate the sector more strictly, electricity demand could fall, potentially leaving consumers to foot the bill for infrastructure upgrades. In addition, the use of clean power in data centre operations is not the only sustainability concern. In October last year, the Minnesota Centre for Environmental Advocacy filed a lawsuit against the city of Pine Island, claiming that the environmental study for the development was vague, initially omitted Google as the end user, and failed to disclose impacts on energy, water, noise, and generators. The initial Alternative Urban Area Review (AUAR) indicated that the new data centre would use approximately 55.7 million gallons of water per year, thereby increasing the city’s total water consumption by approximately 50 per cent. Meanwhile, environmental groups have voiced concerns about the lack of comprehensive groundwater impact analysis. Meanwhile, opponents have questioned whether wastewater discharges may potentially run into the Zumbro River. In a Pine Island survey conducted between 1st and 31st August, 75.8 per cent of participants are against the construction of Project Skyway. While Google has made bold promises to upgrade the grid through clean energy projects, residents and environmental groups have broader concerns about consumer protections and the projects’ environmental impact. So, while Google may be attempting to develop a more “sustainable” data centre, it is failing to win over local residents, who remain concerned about the long-term implications of building a giant AI data centre. artigo.texto: Principais Conclusões - O S-1 da Anthropic, tornado público em 26 de outubro, afirma que a empresa agora arrenda seus próprios data centers e os chips de IA dentro deles, além de alugar poder computacional da Amazon e do Google da Alphabet. - Isso transforma um dos dois maiores clientes de IA da AWS em um rival parcial e limita quanto da crescente conta de computação da Anthropic a AWS pode conquistar além de seu contrato atual. - O compromisso de $110 bilhões da Anthropic com a AWS vai até 2036, enquanto a Amazon gastou $132 bilhões em capex em 2025 e espera cerca de $220 bilhões em 2026. - Os resultados da Amazon de 29 de outubro mostraram o crescimento da AWS acelerando para 39% e sua carteira de pedidos em aberto subindo para $578 bilhões, e o CEO Andy Jassy projeta crescimento da AWS acima de 40% tanto em 2027 quanto em 2028. Amazon (AMZN) tem um novo concorrente na nuvem, e é um de seus maiores clientes. O S-1 da Anthropic, tornado público em 26 de outubro, diz que a criadora do Claude agora arrenda chips de IA diretamente e os opera em data centers arrendados e operados para ela, construídos sob suas próprias especificações. Isso vem além de alugar poder computacional da Amazon e da Alphabet (GOOG). A Anthropic chama o esforço de Anthropic Direct. O S-1 nomeia a Fluidstack, a empresa por trás do acordo de $50 bilhões em data centers no Texas e Nova York que a Anthropic anunciou em novembro de 2025, como uma parceira que desenvolve e opera data centers para ela, e a Anthropic planeja assinar mais contratos de arrendamento. No episódio de 27 de outubro do Prof G Markets, o investidor Paul Kedrosky resumiu o que isso significa: "Eles estão essencialmente replicando a AWS, Amazon Web Services, em ambas as direções." Ele quer dizer que a Anthropic está construindo tanto os produtos que os clientes usam quanto a nuvem por baixo deles. Em sua visão, a Anthropic tem pouca escolha. Depender de seus maiores concorrentes a deixa exposta, então ela precisa fazer investimentos duplicados para parar de depender deles, tanto estrategicamente quanto pela fatia que eles tomam nas vendas através de seus marketplaces de nuvem. Ele espera que os gastos acelerem daqui para frente. Para a AWS, isso significa um grande cliente planejando uma saída parcial. A Amazon Construiu para Esta Demanda A Anthropic se comprometeu com $110 bilhões para a AWS até 2036, vinculados aos chips Trainium da Amazon, e $114,5 bilhões para o Google da Alphabet até 2033, de acordo com a leitura do S-1 pela CNBC. A Amazon gastou pesadamente para estar pronta para contas desse tamanho. Seus gastos de capital mais do que dobraram de $52,7 bilhões em 2023 para $132 bilhões em 2025… E a administração espera cerca de $220 bilhões em capex em caixa em 2026, um número que reafirmou em 29 de outubro. O TIKR Acompanha 60 Analistas na Amazon. Quantos Dizem "Comprar"? Veja a divisão completa das recomendações de Compra, Manter e Venda na Amazon, junto com as estimativas de receita e lucro do Wall Street, tudo em um só lugar. Mais de 500.000 investidores usam o TIKR para pesquisar ações como esta. Veja as Recomendações dos Analistas para a Amazon Essa construção consumiu a maior parte do fluxo de caixa livre da Amazon, que caiu de $32,9 bilhões em 2024 para um magro $7,7 bilhões em 2025… Pela própria métrica da Amazon, o fluxo de caixa livre nos 12 meses até 30 de setembro foi uma saída de $42,4 bilhões, contra $7,6 bilhões três meses antes. Portanto, cada dólar de demanda de IA que a AWS mantém importa para quando esse gasto se pagar. O Anthropic Direct não aparecerá muito no próprio capex da Anthropic, no entanto. O S-1 diz que ela obtém os chips através de arrendamentos de equipamentos e os edifícios também através de arrendamentos, então a construção aparece como compromissos de arrendamento de longo prazo em vez de gastos antecipados. Os Contratos São um Piso A AWS mantém esses $110 bilhões de qualquer maneira. O S-1 da Anthropic diz que seus acordos de computação de longo prazo a obrigam a pagar pela capacidade independentemente de quanto ela realmente use, então, por enquanto, o Anthropic Direct adiciona data centers além do que a Anthropic já deve à Amazon. A AWS também não está sem compradores. Jassy disse em 23 de outubro que a capacidade da AWS está praticamente esgotada até 2027, com uma boa parte de 2028 já comprometida. O potencial de alta é o que encolhe. A carteira de pedidos em aberto da AWS mais do que dobrou de $244 bilhões no final de 2025 para $496 bilhões em 30 de junho de 2026, conforme a Anthropic e a OpenAI adicionaram $100 bilhões ou mais em compromissos cada uma. Esse tipo de salto da Anthropic fica mais difícil de repetir uma vez que ela preenche seus próprios edifícios primeiro. Além disso: a Amazon possui uma grande parte da Anthropic, uma participação que ela contabilizou em $190,4 bilhões em 30 de junho. A Anthropic diz que operar seus próprios data centers pode trazer vantagens de custo de longo prazo. Kedrosky diz que suas margens só se sustentam se o custo computacional de cada token continuar caindo. artigo.texto: AI data center boom supercharges Korean power equipment industry Surging U.S. demand for data centers and grid upgrades is driving strong earnings and exports for Korean power equipment makers HD Hyundai Electric and LS Electric. Two workers monitor the automated process at HD Hyundai Electric's smart transformer factory in Ulsan in an undated photo.HD HYUNDAI ELECTRIC The global rush to build electricity-hungry AI data centers is driving a surge in earnings for Korean electrical equipment manufacturers. HD Hyundai Electric posted an 18.5 percent jump in third quarter revenue this year compared to the same period last year, according to its preliminary earnings report on Tuesday. It earned revenue of 1.18 trillion won ($878 million). Its operating profit also surged 15.1 percent from last year’s third quarter to 284.5 billion won. Its cumulative operating profit for the first nine months reached 829.8 billion won, which puts the company on track to surpass 1 trillion won in annual operating profit for the first time if the momentum continues. LS Electric’s revenue also surged 54.4 percent on year to 1.88 trillion won in the third quarter. Its operating profit more than doubled to 233.5 billion won. The company also extended its streak of quarterly operating profits to 100 consecutive quarters, a run that began in the fourth quarter of 2001. The strong earnings reflect converging demand drivers, particularly in the United States, where rapid expansion of AI data centers and semiconductor plants has coincided with efforts to replace aging power grids. The consequential demand surge has benefited manufacturers of transformers and other electrical equipment. Korea's electrical equipment exports jumped 74 percent from $4.54 billion in 2021 to $7.9 billion last year, according to trade statistics from the Korea International Trade Association. Exports reached a monthly record of $980 million in September, up 39.9 percent from the previous year. “Demand for distribution transformers has grown, particularly in the semiconductor industry, and sales of power distribution equipment have increased in North America,” HD Hyundai Electric said. “Revenue from the battery energy storage system project on Anjwa Island in Shinan County, Jeonnam-Gwangju, which we secured last December, has also begun to contribute significantly to our results.” LS Electric similarly attributed its strong performance to an increasing number of high-value projects, including power solutions for AI data centers and extra-high-voltage transformers. Both companies are ramping up efforts to expand their presence in North America. LS Electric is leveraging its manufacturing presence in Utah and Texas. The company recently signed a long-term deal worth 168.9 billion won to supply high-voltage switchgear to a U.S. tech giant. Its cumulative orders from U.S. fuel cell maker Bloom Energy have surpassed $500 million. HD Hyundai Electric announced plans to invest an additional 198 billion won to expand its Cheongju Power Distribution Campus in North Chungcheong. The expansion is intended to boost production capacity to meet growing North American demand for distribution transformers. “Big Tech customers continue to request additional orders,” an HD Hyundai Electric representative said during an earnings conference call on Tuesday. “We expect revenue from distribution transformers to at least double next year.” Yet concerns about overheating investment in AI data centers could pose a risk to the industry's growth. At least 47 data center projects in the United States were delayed or suspended this year, largely because of financing difficulties and opposition from local communities, according to the Financial Times on Oct. 18. BY NA SANG-HYEON [lee.soojung1@joongang.co.kr] This article was originally written in Korean and translated by a bilingual reporter with the help of generative AI tools. It was then edited by a native English-speaking editor. All AI-assisted translations are reviewed and refined by our newsroom.

artigo.texto: Google’s Suncatcher Prototype Space Data Center Comes Online and Runs AI in Orbit Google’s Suncatcher prototype space data center is operational and communicating with the ground after reaching orbit earlier this month aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 alongside more than 100 other spacecraft. A spokesperson said the satellite is operating nominally. The satellite carries four Google Tensor Processing Units and generates up to 1 kW of power, though it can run only one TPU at a time for about 20 minutes, complicating communications. After roughly three weeks of commissioning, engineers sent their first prompt, asking the onboard Gemma 4 model to write a haiku about space, and also requested a report on orbital conditions. Testing will now examine how the chips handle thermal stress and space radiation, which can cause bit flips that silently corrupt data. Ground tests suggested radiation would affect inference less than training. If successful, Google plans two more satellites in 2027 with greater power and inter-satellite optical links. Suncatcher stands out for planning high-speed links enabling distributed workloads across closely flying satellites. Both Google and SpaceX, in which Alphabet holds a significant stake, depend on a fully reusable Starship, with Suncatcher researchers estimating it would need about 1,800 flights to achieve key cost reductions. The project targets economical orbital infrastructure in the 2030s.

artigo.texto: Politics chat: Data centers are on everyone's minds going into Election Day With days until Election Day, polls show momentum for Democratic candidates and bipartisan distaste for data centers. AYESHA RASCOE, HOST: Heading into this last weekend before Election Day, nearly 50 million people have already voted, either in person or by mail. The total vote in 2022's midterms was 112 million. This year's on pace to beat that number. NPR senior national political correspondent Mara Liasson joins us now. Good morning, Mara. MARA LIASSON, BYLINE: Good morning. RASCOE: So where do things stand this morning from your point of view? LIASSON: Well, Republicans and Democrats agree privately that the House will most likely go to the Democrats. It's unclear about the margin, probably a bigger one than the tiny majority that Republicans have now. Both sides say they are optimistic about the Senate. Of course, someone has to be wrong. Either Democrats will win the Senate majority, or Republicans will hold onto it. The handful of races that are going to determine the majority in the Senate are all still polling within the margin of error. That means that they're too close to call. Democrats will probably pick up seats in the Senate, but it's not clear if they will get the net four pickups they need to take control. And the states that are going to determine that are Texas, Maine, Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, a lot of red states. RASCOE: Campaigns are making their final arguments, and, you know, those are going to vary race to race. In general, though, are there any issues that have risen to the top of voters' minds that stands out to you? LIASSON: Yes, data centers. That was surprising. In the beginning of the cycle, it wasn't clear they would be such a big issue. States had been competing to get data centers to come to their states, but it turns out they are very unpopular. That sentiment is bipartisan. It's an example of the kind of economic populism that we see converging from the left and right. It's why you saw Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon appear at the same anti-AI conference. And data centers is the way that AI is most present to voters in their own communities. Majorities don't want them there. And it's caused some pretty dramatic flip-flops. Incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott courted data centers for years. All of a sudden, now he's for a moratorium. And I think they've become a proxy for the backlash against billionaires. You know, the rich get richer while you can't afford gas. And the debate over the data centers also illustrates another big theme of the campaign, which is that Donald Trump is on the opposite side of majority popular opinion. On issue after issue, this is true - on Iran, on tariffs. On data centers, he says he's for them. He's called them a golden goose for the economy. He was in Ohio in October at a rally with Republican incumbent Senator Jon Husted. He said, we want data centers. He says, you can't turn them off. They'll go to China. RASCOE: October has come and gone. Were there any so-called October surprises? LIASSON: Well, I would say the closest thing to an October surprise is the double Dan Sullivan situation in Alaska. The Republican governor there says he's starting an investigation. President Trump has asked his Department of Justice to investigate how Daniel J. Sullivan got on the ballot. The incumbent senator is Dan S. Sullivan. There was some reporting in The New York Times that the Mary Peltola campaign - she's the Democratic candidate - was deeply involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan. Peltola denies that. The big question is, is any of this illegal? RASCOE: I mean, that is a big question. Alaska's Supreme Court ruled in June that both Sullivans could appear on the ballot. And this is far from the first example of political parties, for lack of a better term, gaming the vote. LIASSON: That's right. It happens a lot. Both parties do it. There are some examples this cycle. And one of them in Ohio, a Republican group, spent more than $2 million to promote a socialist candidate in the Senate race named Greg Levy. They're hoping to pull away votes from the Democratic candidate, former Senator Sherrod Brown. So sometimes it's a person with a similar name, like in Alaska. Sometimes it's a person who's on the extreme of the opposite party, and the other party backs them in an effort to try to split the vote. Remember when Trump's allies tried to get Kanye West to run for president in hopes that he could split the Black vote? It's just unclear what, if any, laws these kinds of political shenanigans would break. RASCOE: And yet the Justice Department is moving forward with its lawsuit about this, right? LIASSON: That's right. They're asking a judge to separate all ballots in Alaska showing votes for the second Dan Sullivan, Dan J. Sullivan, until it can be determined if voters really meant to vote for him. Alaska officials say that would be impossible. The Trump administration has also filed a lawsuit to block the certification of the Alaska Senate race in case the Republican loses, but Trump doesn't have a good track record in court on these kinds of suits. Last week, U.S. judge Trina Thompson ordered the administration to stop threatening state and local election officials with prosecution if they didn't refuse to issue ballots to people the administration says may be ineligible to vote. So this all adds up to what Trump's critics argue is an effort to try to take control of elections, overturn the results if they don't go his way. RASCOE: That's NPR's Mara Liasson. Mara, thank you so much. LIASSON: You're welcome. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. artigo.texto: Casablanca – A battery technology developed by Singapore-based KVI and involving Moroccan scientist and electrochemist Rachid Yazami has achieved a charge from 10% to 70% in just 3.7 minutes, with the company reporting a full charge in seven minutes. KVI announced the results on Thursday, saying it used its proprietary Non-Linear Voltammetry (NLV) technology to charge an individual lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cell. The company said the cell maintained a temperature below 50 degrees Celsius throughout the test. Yazami, who founded KVI and is widely known for inventing the graphite anode used in modern lithium-ion batteries, explained how the new invention works. Unlike conventional charging systems that primarily regulate the electrical current supplied to a battery, KVI’s NLV technology uses a stepwise, voltage-controlled approach. The system allows the current to respond to changes in the battery’s electrochemical characteristics during charging. “The challenge is not simply to push more electricity into a battery in less time,” Yazami said, explaining that the technology focuses on understanding how batteries respond during charging to deliver energy more effectively. Yazami also described the voltage profile produced by NLV as a unique fingerprint that reflects the battery’s response throughout the charging process. The company said the technology can work with different lithium-ion chemistries, capacities and formats. Its potential applications include mobile phones, power tools and electric vehicles. Read also: Gotion to Launch Morocco’s First Battery Gigafactory in Kenitra the Week of October 20 Beyond charging speed, KVI said its technology incorporates patented diagnostic capabilities to monitor battery health and detect early signs of internal short circuits. The company’s research has also demonstrated potential improvements in battery lifespan. Electro Mobility Holding Singapore is preparing to commercialize the technology through NLV-controlled charging systems, with electric vehicles among its priority markets. The company also plans to expand its research and development activities in Singapore as part of a broader international initiative covering battery technology, charging infrastructure and electric mobility. The technology could also serve electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, known as eVTOLs, by reducing charging times between flights. On October 28, Japanese eVTOL developer SkyDrive signed a memorandum of understanding with Singapore-based KVI to explore the application of the technology in electric aircraft. The announcement comes as competition over faster electric vehicle charging intensifies. Chinese automaker BYD announced in March 2026 that its second-generation Blade Battery and FLASH Charging system could charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes and reach 97% in nine minutes. Global electric vehicle sales exceeded 20 million in 2025, according to figures cited by KVI, which expects the number to reach 23 million in 2026. Yazami previously discussed plans to transfer KVI’s battery expertise to Morocco under a proposed KVI Maroc initiative, according to a 2021 report by SciDev.Net. Meanwhile, Morocco has advanced its own LFP battery storage projects, including OCP Green Energy’s large-scale installation in Benguerir, which uses technology supplied by Envision.

artigo.texto: Pakistan’s proposed $2.25 billion battery Giga-factory presents a question that goes well beyond manufacturing lithium-ion cells: can an economy constrained by foreign-exchange shortages, expensive electricity and a shallow industrial base turn an emerging energy market into a globally competitive manufacturing industry? The opportunity is real. So are the risks. The difference between the two will be determined not by the investment headline, but by the economics beneath it. According to The News International, Margalla Heavy Industries Limited (MHIL), a military-owned enterprise, has signed an agreement with Chinese partners and a Pakistani private investor for a battery manufacturing facility at Taxila. Engineering Development Board (EDB) chief executive Hamad Ali Mansoor says the building is ready and machinery installed, but production awaits government approval of a dedicated battery manufacturing policy. The identities of the investors have not been disclosed publicly in the reporting reviewed. That distinction matters. An announced investment is not the same as capital deployed; installed machinery is not proof of commercially viable production; and domestic manufacturing does not automatically translate into economic gain. The project deserves serious consideration, but its scale makes independent scrutiny essential. Pakistan has a compelling reason to develop battery manufacturing. Households and businesses are adopting solar power and storage partly because grid electricity has become expensive. Industrial users need reliable power, while electric mobility could create another market for cells, packs and associated electronics. Batteries can also help manage fluctuations in renewable generation and supply electricity during peak periods. Yet the country’s electricity market is not expanding in a straight line. Pakistan’s Economic Survey 2024-25 recorded electricity consumption of 80,111 gigawatt-hours during July-March FY2025, a 3.6 per cent decline from the corresponding period a year earlier. High tariffs, off-grid solar adoption, conservation and subdued industrial activity were among the factors identified. This is not an argument against batteries. It is a warning that demand must be modelled around changing consumer behaviour, not simply extrapolated from population and growth projections. The EDB estimates that battery energy storage demand could reach 100,000 megawatts by June 2030 if GDP growth reaches at least 5 per cent, and 80,000 megawatts if growth remains below 3 per cent. It also estimates that grid stabilisation alone could require 3,000-5,000 megawatts of storage. These are substantial projections, but the public reporting does not provide enough methodological detail to independently validate them. There is also a technical issue that cannot be brushed aside. Megawatts measure the rate at which a battery can deliver power; megawatt-hours measure how much energy it stores. A 1,000-megawatt storage system capable of discharging for four hours requires 4,000 megawatt-hours of storage. A system delivering the same power for two hours has half that energy capacity. Battery-cell production is generally discussed in terms of energy capacity, such as gigawatt-hours per year. Until the project’s proposed output, storage duration and production units are clearly specified, comparisons between projected demand and factory capacity remain incomplete. The government needs an independently reviewed demand model separating residential backup systems, commercial and industrial storage, grid-scale installations and electric-vehicle batteries. These markets overlap, but they are not interchangeable. Each has different technical requirements, purchasing cycles, price sensitivities and potential customers. A forecast that combines them without transparent assumptions risks turning an ambitious market estimate into the justification for an oversized factory. The most immediate industrial opportunity may lie in replacing finished-product imports while building the capabilities required for more sophisticated manufacturing. Pakistan imported an estimated 1.25 gigawatt-hours of lithium-ion battery storage packs in 2024, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. Its Analysis warns that widespread adoption of decentralised storage could also intensify financial pressures on a grid already burdened by fixed costs and long-term power purchase commitments. This creates a two-sided economic challenge. Domestic batteries could reduce dependence on imported equipment, but they will not solve Pakistan’s power-sector problems on their own. If consumers leave the grid because electricity is unaffordable, the resulting reduction in sales can push fixed costs onto those who remain connected. Storage policy must therefore be coordinated with tariff reform, grid modernisation and a more sustainable structure for recovering electricity costs. Nor should every import be treated as a loss that localisation automatically corrects. Imports give consumers access to established technologies, competitive prices and reliable products. Replacing them with more expensive domestic goods behind permanent tariff barriers could transfer costs to households and businesses without creating a genuinely productive industry. The test is whether Pakistani manufacturers can progressively compete on cost, quality and reliability, not whether they can sell under protection. Pakistan's proposed $2.25 billion battery Giga-factory offers an opportunity to reduce import dependence and build industrial capacity, but investment commitments, technology transfer, competitive production and export performance will determine whether it becomes manufacturing breakthrough or an expensive industrial gamble China’s participation offers a potential shortcut into a technically demanding industry. artigo.texto: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has said that some Michigan voters are "deathly afraid" of the rapid growth of data centers. Artificial intelligence and the rapid construction of data centers have emerged as key issues ahead of the midterm elections. Citizens across the country have raised concerns about their potential impact on electricity bills, water consumption, and noise disrupting nearby neighborhoods. Speaking on CBS News' 60 Minutes, El Sayed discussed the most important issues facing Michiganders that he had witnessed during his campaign. "Had you asked me five years ago, I would have said healthcare. It still is really really high on people's minds. I think right now we are barreling toward a world where the most important issue I hear about every day is AI," he said. Read More on News He said that AI could transform the economy so rapidly that society would be unable to adjust, and warned of the risks of the technology escaping human control and being used by terrorists to develop a biological weapon or fueling an arms race that threatens humanity. "All of these outcomes are really really quite scary. I hear it in so many different ways," he said. El-Sayed added that students were fearful of the disruption the technology could bring to the jobs market, and cited rural voters who were concerned about the impact of data centers on utility bills. "These are these are issues that people are deathly afraid of and it shows up in just all kinds of ways," he said. El-Sayed is competing against Republican Mike Rogers in a closely watched Senate contest that will help decide the balance of power in Congress. This is a developing story. More to follow.

artigo.texto: New Delhi: Scaling up long-duration energy storage (LDES) will be critical for India to achieve its target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel energy capacity by 2030, the India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA) said in a press release shared with BioEnergy Times. The report was prepared in association with Customized Energy Solutions (CES). The report, titled Long-Duration Energy Storage: Global Outlook and India’s Deployment Pathway, identifies the proposed viability gap funding (VGF) framework for fiscal 2027-28 as a key mechanism to accelerate investment in and deployment of long-duration storage technologies. Highlighting the challenges of integrating renewable energy into the grid, the report said India curtailed 2.3 terawatt-hours (TWh) of solar power over eight months in 2025 due to grid and storage constraints. It said greater storage capacity would help absorb surplus renewable electricity and make it available during periods of high demand or lower generation. Globally, the Long Duration Energy Storage Council estimates that around 8 terawatts (TW), equivalent to 140 TWh, of LDES capacity will be required by 2040. In comparison, only 117 GW was operational in 2025. Meeting the projected requirement would require nearly $4 trillion in investment and could generate annual system-wide savings of around $540 billion. In India, the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has projected a requirement of 34.5 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) by FY2027. While 9.3 GWh has been commissioned, another 195 GWh of projects have been awarded or are under tender. However, the existing project pipeline is largely focused on short-duration storage solutions. The report identifies several technologies that could address different storage requirements. Flow batteries are suited to daily storage cycles of eight to 12 hours, while iron-air batteries can provide multi-day storage. Pumped hydro, compressed air and thermal energy storage could also cater to large-scale and industrial applications. IESA said India currently lacks a formal statutory definition of long-duration energy storage and a dedicated funding mechanism for projects offering eight hours or more of storage. Debmalya Sen, president of IESA, said long-duration storage would help improve renewable energy utilisation, grid stability and power system resilience. He called for supportive policies, innovative commercial models and technology-neutral investment to accelerate deployment. The report recommended collaboration among policymakers, regulators, industry participants and investors to develop suitable policy and financing frameworks to expand long-duration energy storage capacity.

artigo.texto: Bess Atwell announces new album Cut A Figure inspired by spontaneous move to Canada London indie-folk artist Bess Atwell has announced her fourth album, Cut A Figure, out 5 February 2027 via Nettwerk, and shared lead single “Glass” with a video. She has also confirmed 2027 world tour dates. Atwell explained that the album title comes from a line in the lead single, "Glass": "I knew I wanted to name the album after a line in this song as it feels like the heart of the record. Sometimes, an eagerness to be seen and understood can have the opposite effect – you can be so transparent that you end up invisible.” She added that as a teenager she took a personality test in which participants imagine a cube: “All my friends and family pictured various different sizes and colours, while I saw a transparent glass box floating in space.” The new record follows 2024’s Light Sleeper and was shaped by a spontaneous move to Canada, where Atwell lived for nine months in Quebec. It is her first for the Vancouver label Nettwerk, home to Alice Phoebe Lou, Night Tapes, and Ladytron. Cut A Figure was produced by Chris Coady at his Glendale, California studio. Coady has worked with numerous artists, including Beach House, Yuck, Future Islands, Show Me the Body, IAN SWEET, and DIIV. The 2027 tour includes UK dates in Glasgow, Birmingham, and London, where an album launch show takes place at the Barbican on 6 February. North American dates run through March, followed by Australia, further UK and Ireland shows in April, and European dates in May. artigo.texto: Intel Slides as Weak Q4 Outlook Overshadows Data Center Growth Intel Corp. (INTC, Financials), the semiconductor manufacturer, delivered stronger third-quarter results but issued a weaker fourth-quarter outlook as a factory shutdown, PC weakness and supply constraints weighed on expectations. Third quarter sales was $16.5 billion, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.52 and gross margin of 44.1%. Data Center and AI sales was $7.3 billion with operating profit of $3 billion, Intel's best sector revenue increase in 15 years. But guidance for the fourth quarter underwhelmed. Intel predicts revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, non-GAAP EPS of $0.25 and gross margin of 38 percent. An accident at its Fab 28 plant in Israel would likely affect fourth-quarter sales by around $300 million and lower gross margin by about 200 basis points. Intel also sees its client computing sales dropping by more than 20% quarter-over-quarter, as the PC correction intensifies. Looking ahead, management sees healthy demand for server CPUs, forecasting the addressable market may grow from roughly $40 billion to more than $200 billion over a five-year period. The next driver is recovery at Fab 28 and Intel's ability to turn increased server demand into better free cash flow.

artigo.texto: Mercado de carbono: indústria terá de começar a medir emissões a partir de 2027; veja setores O governo federal definiu o cronograma de implementação das obrigações de mensuração, relato e verificação (MRV) de emissões de gases de efeito estufa no mercado regulado de carbono brasileiro. A medida foi estabelecida pela Portaria nº 3.199, publicada pelo Ministério da Fazenda nAa quinta-feira (29), e prevê a entrada gradual de setores da economia no Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE) a partir de 2027. Na primeira etapa, com início em 2027, estão incluídos os setores de alumínio, usinas integradas de ferro e aço, cimento, exploração e produção de petróleo e gás natural, alguns segmentos da indústria química, mineração de minério de ferro e bauxita, papel e celulose e vidro. A segunda etapa começa até 2029 e contempla cerâmica, usinas semi-integradas de ferro e aço, outros segmentos da indústria química, alimentos e bebidas, mineração de outras substâncias minerais, refino de petróleo e setor elétrico. Já a terceira fase, prevista para começar até 2031, incluirá os transportes rodoviário, ferroviário e aquaviário. A obrigação de monitoramento será aplicada a operadores com emissões anuais a partir de 10 mil toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (tCO₂e), o que representa menos de 1% dos CNPJs do país. Empresas com emissões superiores a 25 mil toneladas anuais também estarão sujeitas às obrigações previstas no Plano Nacional de Alocação (PNA), após 2030. Cada etapa terá um ciclo de preparação de quatro anos. O primeiro será dedicado à elaboração do plano de monitoramento, os dois seguintes ao acompanhamento das emissões e o quarto à consolidação dos dados para o PNA. O que muda para as empresas A publicação da portaria não exige a apresentação imediata de relatórios nem estabelece limites de emissão ou custos nesta fase inicial. O objetivo dos primeiros anos será preparar as empresas para medir e reportar suas emissões de maneira padronizada. O teto global de emissões e a distribuição das Cotas Brasileiras de Emissões (CBEs) serão definidos no Plano Nacional de Alocação, com vigência prevista a partir de 2030. Na largada, a distribuição das cotas será integralmente gratuita. O Ministério da Fazenda também prevê estruturar, ainda em 2026, uma Câmara de Assuntos Regulatórios com os setores da primeira etapa. O governo pretende realizar em novembro consultas públicas sobre os programas brasileiros de Mensuração, Relato e Verificação (PB-MRV) e de Compensação de Emissões (PBCE). A implementação do mercado regulado está prevista na Lei nº 15.042/2024. Com o sistema, o Brasil busca estruturar um mecanismo de precificação de carbono e avançar no cumprimento de seu compromisso internacional de alcançar a neutralidade das emissões até 2050.

artigo.texto: China exempts sodium-ion batteries from tax as Hina targets 10 GWh commerical EV push A Chinese electric heavy truck equipped with a sodium-ion battery retained more than 90% of its usable capacity at minus 40°C during testing, according to FAW Jiefang, providing evidence of the chemistry’s low-temperature performance in heavy-duty vehicles. Hina Battery is expanding its commercial vehicle push, with a planned 10 GWh production base in Wuhan and a partnership to develop electric sanitation trucks. The expansion comes as China introduces a consumption tax on specified lithium-ion batteries while exempting qualifying sodium-ion batteries through 2028. The policy gives the alternative chemistry a temporary tax advantage, even as falling lithium prices have narrowed its potential cost advantage over lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. China creates a tax gap between lithium and sodium batteries China’s Ministry of Finance, General Administration of Customs and State Taxation Administration issued Announcement No. 20 (2026) on July 16, revising consumption tax treatment for several battery categories. From September 1, 2026, specified lithium-ion batteries became subject to a 2% consumption tax, rising to 4% on September 1, 2027. Sodium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries and fuel cells are exempt through December 31, 2028, provided they meet applicable national standards. The tax difference comes as lower lithium prices put pressure on sodium-ion’s potential cost advantage. On October 28, battery-grade lithium carbonate averaged around 97,000 yuan (13,500 USD) per tonne, while square LFP cells for electric vehicles averaged 0.41 yuan (0.057 USD) per Wh on October 22. The exemption gives qualifying sodium-ion batteries a tax advantage, but does not establish that they are cheaper to manufacture than LFP batteries. Sodium-ion also offers a different raw-material supply profile. Sodium-based feedstocks are more geographically distributed than lithium resources, although the downstream supply chain remains heavily concentrated in China, including cell, cathode and hard-carbon production. Hina takes sodium-ion technology into commercial fleets Hina signed an agreement with Wuhan’s Jiangxia District on October 14 to establish a sodium-ion battery production base with a planned annual capacity of 10 GWh. Signed during the fourth National Sodium Battery Symposium, the agreement covers a first phase of 3 GWh. Construction is scheduled to begin in early 2027, with initial production expected before the end of that year. Under a separate agreement, Hina and Chengli Special Automobile Group will develop sodium-ion-powered sanitation vehicles, including refuse collection, hook-lift, dust-suppression and food-waste collection trucks. The partners expect to submit an initial chassis approval application in early 2027. After prototype development, they plan demonstration vehicles, followed by vehicle approval and small-volume orders. Wuhan is expected to host the initial demonstrations. Sanitation and engineering trucks offer potential early applications because their chassis can accommodate larger battery systems and their defined operating routes allow performance to be assessed under specific working conditions. Passenger cars face different requirements, particularly for energy density and packaging. Heavy trucks provide a proving ground for sodium-ion batteries Energy density remains a limitation compared with established lithium-ion batteries. Hina’s published specifications for its sodium-ion products list a gravimetric energy density of at least 145 Wh/kg and an operating temperature range of minus 40 to 80 degrees Celsius. The company has already tested the technology in heavy-duty vehicles. In June 2026, a battery-electric FAW Jiefang J6P tractor equipped with a 339 kWh Hina sodium-ion battery completed nearly seven months of testing and more than 15,000 km of driving. At minus 40 degrees Celsius, FAW Jiefang reported that the battery retained more than 90% of its usable capacity. In August, Hina and Tonly Heavy Industries delivered an electric mining truck equipped with a 676 kWh sodium-ion battery system to the Tangshan Sanyou mine in Hebei Province. These deployments show sodium-ion technology entering heavy-duty applications, where low-temperature performance, frequent charging and high battery utilisation can be important. They do not establish its suitability for every electric vehicle segment. Hard-carbon anodes remain a cost challenge Sodium is abundant, but inexpensive raw materials do not automatically translate into cheaper battery cells. Commercial sodium-ion batteries commonly use hard-carbon anodes made from coal, biomass and other carbon-rich feedstocks. Producing hard carbon with the required structure and electrochemical properties involves controlled processing, adding cost and manufacturing complexity. Sodium-ion batteries have yet to establish a consistent cost advantage over LFP. Their lower energy density may also require larger or heavier battery packs to deliver comparable vehicle range, making their commercial viability application-dependent. China sets new safety requirements for sodium-ion batteries China is also establishing technical requirements for sodium-ion batteries. GB/T 48072-2026, published on August 28, specifies safety requirements for sodium-ion cells and batteries used in electrical energy storage systems. It is scheduled to take effect on March 1, 2027. The standard covers stationary energy storage, not automotive traction batteries, and is not an electric vehicle approval standard. Separately, the tax exemption requires qualifying products to meet applicable national standards.

artigo.texto: A fabricante norte-americana de semicondutores está em negociações para assegurar milhares de milhões de dólares em garantias de financiamento de dívida à fornecedora de computação na nuvem Nscale, viabilizando a construção de um novo centro de dados dedicado à Anthropic na Virgínia Ocidental. A informação foi avançada na quinta-feira pelo The Information e posteriormente corroborada pela agência Bloomberg, expondo o esforço do setor da inteligência artificial para manter a expansão física ativa perante o receio dos investidores quanto ao volume de capital exigido. O primeiro edifício deste complexo tem uma capacidade projetada de 460 megawatts (unidade que mede a potência elétrica instantânea disponível para alimentar dezenas de milhares de servidores em simultâneo) e já conta com um contrato de 44,6 mil milhões de dólares (cerca de 39,8 mil milhões de € à taxa de câmbio atual) assinado pela Anthropic, segundo os documentos de entrada em bolsa da Nscale. A infraestrutura deverá operar com a próxima geração de processadores da marca, numa altura em que a Nvidia avança com a produção em massa do hardware Vera Rubin. As duas empresas discutem ainda um segundo acordo, avaliado em aproximadamente 45 mil milhões de dólares (cerca de 40,2 mil milhões de €), para erguer um edifício adicional no mesmo recinto. O mecanismo de garantia residual e a exposição financeira da Nvidia Ao contrário do apoio prestado anteriormente a outros fornecedores de nuvem, que se limitava ao arrendamento de equipamento e à aquisição de chips, este acordo coloca a tecnológica como fiadora direta das obras e do fornecimento elétrico do complexo na Virgínia Ocidental. O modelo em cima da mesa funciona como uma garantia de valor residual: caso a Nscale entre em incumprimento nos pagamentos da construção, a Nvidia assume temporariamente o controlo das instalações e fica encarregue de procurar um novo comprador e um novo inquilino para o espaço. A fabricante tem atuado como um dos principais pilares financeiros desta indústria, somando cerca de 170 mil milhões de dólares (cerca de 151,7 mil milhões de €) em investimentos e linhas de apoio ao crédito concedidas a grandes clientes e a empresas de nuvem especializadas em IA. Desse montante global faz parte uma fatia de mil milhões de dólares (cerca de 892 milhões de €) em financiamento convertível atribuída à própria Nscale em setembro. Para a empresa liderada por Jensen Huang, assegurar a viabilidade da obra protege também a encomenda de um cliente estratégico. A Anthropic figura entre os maiores compradores mundiais de capacidade computacional, mas tem distribuído o seu orçamento de infraestrutura por vários fabricantes de semicondutores, pelo que o envolvimento direto da criadora do Claude ajuda a explicar a disponibilidade da Nvidia para assumir o risco imobiliário e energético do projeto. Atrasos operacionais da Nscale e pressão nos mercados de capitais A viabilização deste financiamento ganha peso num momento em que a Nscale prepara a sua oferta pública inicial (IPO) com o objetivo de atingir uma avaliação até 35 mil milhões de dólares (cerca de 31,2 mil milhões de €), apesar das dúvidas do mercado sobre a sua capacidade de execução. Em agosto, a empresa tinha cerca de 25.000 processadores avançados de inteligência artificial em funcionamento, uma pequena fração face aos quase 500.000 chips que planeia instalar. O terreno na Virgínia Ocidental também já enfrentou obstáculos próprios: o escoamento de águas provenientes do estaleiro de obras inundou habitações vizinhas em mais do que uma ocasião, e a certificação estatal só foi atribuída em setembro após vários meses de negociações. A estas dificuldades nos Estados Unidos soma-se um revés recente na Europa, já que em outubro a Microsoft cancelou o acordo para um centro de dados da Nscale no Reino Unido depois de o fornecimento de energia da rede elétrica para essa localização em Inglaterra ter sido adiado para a década de 2030. O ceticismo dos mercados afeta igualmente todo o segmento das chamadas neoclouds (fornecedoras que alugam poder de computação para IA sem terem um negócio principal gerador de liquidez a suportar a operação). De acordo com dados da CNBC citados na peça, as ações da CoreWeave, da Nebius e da IREN acumularam quedas superiores a 30% durante o mês de outubro até à semana passada. A própria Anthropic enfrenta escrutínio financeiro após ter submetido esta semana o pedido para entrar em bolsa: a gestora de ativos Blackstone alertou os investidores de que a empresa de IA poderá receber uma notação de crédito abaixo do grau de investimento (classificação financeira conhecida como dívida de alto risco ou junk) após o IPO, o que agravaria os seus custos de endividamento e forçaria a dependência contínua de parceiros mais capitalizados para garantir a sua dívida.

artigo.texto: Questions remain after city council tightens oversight of data centers with 9-2 vote SAN ANTONIO - The city has adopted new rules that tighten oversight of data centers, a move supporters say will give residents more say in projects that can affect neighborhoods, while critics warn the changes could push jobs and investment elsewhere. City Council voted 9-2 to require public review and council approval for new data center projects. The rules took effect immediately and apply to the industry’s footprint in San Antonio, where there are 75 data centers operating or planned for operation. The changes also add restrictions on where data centers can be built and the rules they must follow. A key piece of the new policy requires projects to go before City Council for public approval before moving forward in the process. “We’re able to deliver today as the largest city in Texas to push on the best regulations possible here in the state of Texas,” Ric Galvan said after the vote. Supporters say the new rules give residents a voice amid concerns about water use, electricity demand and noise. But critics of the tighter regulations say the restrictions could drive jobs and investment out of the city. Officials with District 6 and the city’s zoning and policy staff said projects with existing permits can move forward. Councilman Marc Whyte said he understands why some residents are worried about data centers near their homes. “We know that there’s a lot of fear out there about these data centers. People don’t want them placed right in the middle of their neighborhoods, and I understand that,” Whyte said. Questions remain about whether the new rules will protect communities from issues other parts of the country have faced, whether the regulations could discourage businesses from building in San Antonio, and how the new process will work for projects already in the planning stages.

artigo.texto: Data centers have become one of the nation’s defining political issues ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. As tech giants invest hundreds of billions of dollars to build behemoth facilities and use vast amounts of power to support their artificial intelligence race, communities have pushed back. Candidates on the federal, state and local levels have responded to data center opposition by proposing stringent regulations on the industry — and by painting their opponents as data center supporters. This contentious issue could influence the control of Congress and reshape statehouses across the country. But for all the focus on data centers on the campaign trail, industry experts say the election’s actual impact on the development boom may be less widespread than the rhetoric would suggest. In Congress, even if a wave of anti-data center Democrats take control of both chambers, they would still struggle to pass significant legislation that could receive the signature of President Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of the industry. In many states, candidates on both sides of the aisle are supporting stricter data center rules — meaning the industry is in for a tougher road no matter who wins. But there are state-level races in the key digital infrastructure markets of Texas, Pennsylvania and Georgia where candidates have staked out different positions, and the election could determine how much data center development will be allowed to move forward. Just in those three states, Morgan Stanley estimates the planned development of 284 data centers totaling more than 33 gigawatts of capacity are at risk pending the results of these races. “I don't think at the federal level the policy is going to shift much,” MOCA Economics Chief Economist Brandon Michalski told Bisnow. “If we go to the state level, that shifts dramatically and could change the trajectory significantly.” The Battle For Capitol Hill From Ohio and Michigan to Wisconsin, Texas and Maine, data centers have emerged as a major campaign issue in high-profile House and Senate races ahead of this week’s midterms. Data centers are deeply unpopular, and congressional candidates from both parties have made proposals to rein in development or limit its impacts a core element of their campaigns as voters voice growing concerns over electricity costs, environmental impacts and the broader consequences of the AI data center boom. The trend is especially visible in political advertising. As of the beginning of October, House and Senate campaigns had spent more than $29M on ads mentioning data centers, almost always negatively, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Bisnow. Although opposition to data centers cuts across party lines, Democrats have more aggressively nationalized the issue, contrasting calls for oversight of the sector with the Trump administration’s support for accelerating AI infrastructure development. Prominent congressional Democrats have already proposed measures like a national data center moratorium and released an investigation arguing that hyperscalers aren’t paying their fair share of grid costs. Now, party leaders are signaling their intent to make more aggressive oversight of the industry a prominent part of their policy agenda following the midterms, particularly if the party gains control of one or both houses of Congress. Last week, the Senate’s top Democratic tax writer announced plans to pursue an additional excise tax on data centers while eliminating the industry’s ability to tap a range of existing tax benefits tied to depreciation, research spending, opportunity zones and REIT structures. Although Republicans have also pursued measures aimed at addressing voter concerns over data centers driving up electricity prices, GOP leaders have privately acknowledged that data centers have become a winning issue for Democrats. The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned major technology and AI firms in August that Democrats were successfully making data centers the “centerpiece” of the Senate race in Ohio and that deteriorating public sentiment toward the industry was becoming a broader risk to Republican candidates specifically. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle,” the letter warned. The data center industry has taken notice of this partisan dynamic. AI infrastructure super PAC Leading the Future and connected groups have spent significantly more supporting Republicans than Democrats, according to Forbes, while hyperscalers and AI giants like OpenAI have reportedly ramped up lobbying in anticipation of more aggressive Democratic oversight of data center development and the AI trade. Investors and analysts focused on the data center industry have similarly warned that the potential for Democratic victories in the House and Senate poses a threat to the industry’s growth and would bring greater regulatory and political risk. “There will be congressional hearings. There will be investigations,” said Brian Gardner, chief Washington policy strategist at Stifel, according to Reuters. “You never know where that stuff leads, and there can be negative headlines.” Yet despite the rhetoric and the flood of money pouring into congressional races, not everyone is convinced that even a Democratic sweep would materially change the federal regulatory environment for data centers. A report published this week by MOCA Economics examining data center construction spending projected that Democratic control of at least one chamber would be a “nothingburger for policy.” Michalski, who authored the report, said Democrats could introduce more restrictive bills, but Trump’s veto power would make measures such as a national moratorium, sweeping new grid cost requirements or additional tax burdens extremely difficult to enact.
